en.full: 64-11204012-KAT (Culture) Enhancing national capacities for the effective implementation of the World Heritage Convention 1-4

en.value:
JUSTIFICATION
	1. Regular monitoring need for Nepal's WH properties is reflected in frequent requests for interventions/changes related to properties
	2. Need to monitor the implementation of the IMP for Kathmandu Valley and its possible review to tackle emerging challenges, including disaster risk reduction and tourism initiatives for sustainable heritage management;
	3. Need to increase the awareness/participation of communities in heritage protection to address challenges of living with and around WH properties, targeting members of communities who are unacquainted or not well-informed of the opportunities, processes and protection needs of the properties as community assets
	4. Need to assist the national authorities in the process of nominating new sites for inclusion in the World Heritage List
	5. Little understanding of the role of cultural heritage as a contributor to the sustainable development of local communities
	
	MODALITIES
	1. Technical assistance in monitoring and assessment study
	2. Capacity building and awareness raising workshops
	3. Exploring extra-budgetary funding for
	3.a Integrating disaster risk reduction strategies in management plans and its implementation
	3.b Up scaling self-sustaining initiatives with community
	3.b.1 Survey to review Manual for traditional home-owners for Kathmandu Valley and possible new edition
	3.b.2 Exploring the potential of heritage to contribute to sustainable development
	3.c Establishing coherent information /knowledge management system (for Lumbini in view of establishing documentation centre)
	4. Strengthening partnership with local municipal offices, among others for promoting the application of UNESCO Recommendation on Historic Urban Landscape (HUL), especially in Kathmandu Valley
	5. Strengthening inter-ministerial coordination to enhance understanding of and ensure support for WH protection at different levels
	6. Cluster and regional exchanges for learning from international experiences
	7. Leaflet Publication promoting World Heritage properties in Nepal and re-production of translated operational guidelines in Nepali
	8. Advocating for Nepal's possible accession to Hague Convention and its two protocols
	
	TARGET GROUPS
	• Policy makers
	• Site managers
	• Community at large/ civil society and community leaders
	
	RISK
	• Possible interventions impacting the OUV of the World Heritage properties
	• Loosening of credibility of UNESCO's action in the field

en.full: Partnerships: Research and Analytical -INTERNATIONAL CRISIS GROUP

en.value: The Partnerships: Research and Analytical initiative consolidates eight new and existing agreements that support and enhance strategic partnerships with leading research institutions in fragility, peace, conflict and development issues. The partnership will: ensure continued access to international cutting edge research, analysis and intellectual policy expertise ; ability to draw on international best practice and lessons learned from fragile, complex and conflict affected environments; provide an opportunity to input and steer direction at international policy discussion level; access to international products and materials including guidance notes, analysis and toolkits. This initiative contributes to two of the Crisis Prevention, Stabilisation and Recovery (CPSR) Group's objectives: international and whole of government engagement by leveraging best practice and analysis for the  Australia aid program from strategic partnerships; and strategic advice guidance that draws on cross-Agency experience, international analysis and lessons learned from fragile, complex and conflict affected areas. The total value of this initiative is $11.9 million over 8 years, starting 2008-09.

en.full: South Asia Water Initiative (SAWI)

en.value: The South Asia Water Initiative (SAWI) aims to promote regional cooperation in the sustainable management of the water resources of the Himalayan rivers to address the challenges of development and climate change.  The program will be structured around five key focus areas: (1) Ganges Basin, (2) Brahmaputra Basin, (3) Indus Basin, (4) Sundarbans Landscape, and (5) Regional Cooperation. To promote more effective and cooperative water resources management, SAWI will facilitate multi-stakeholder dialogue and policy deliberation; enhance knowledge and capacity on issues of regional, and in particular trans-boundary water resources management and climate adaptation; and promote cooperative actions such as policy reforms, institutional development, and investment in water resources management. The total value of this multi-country initiative is $9.0 million over 5 years, starting 2008-09.

en.full: International Planned Parenthood Federation (IPPF) South Asia Strategic Plan 2010-2015

en.value:
This initiative supports the International Planned Parenthood Federation (IPPF) South Asia Strategic Plan 2010-2015 and forms part of the Government's commitment to advance Millennium Development Goal (MDG) 5 (improve maternal health) in South Asia. The South Asia region has the highest rates of maternal and neonatal deaths and unmet demand for contraception in the Asia-Pacific. The funding of this initiative helps reduce maternal deaths in South Asia by improving equitable access for underserved groups to a range of reproductive health services and education including family planning. These goals are met by IPPF's South Asia Strategic Plan which focuses on 4 priority areas: 1) ensuring young people have access and rights to services and education; 2) reducing social, cultural and economic barriers that impede access; 3) HIV/AIDS prevention and care; and 4) reducing unsafe abortion. The total value of this multi-country initiative is up to $11 million over 3 years, starting 2010-11.

en.full: USRP Project for Bhutanese Refugee

en.value: After languishing in refugee camps in eastern Nepal for 18 years, 108,000 registered Bhutanese refugees became eligible for third country resettlement in late 2007 due to the concerted efforts of a Core Group of resettlement countries, UNHCR and the Government of Nepal.  IOM assists in the resettlement of Bhutanese refugees from Nepal to the United States (and other countries) by 1) interviewing refugees and completing US Government forms; 2) conducting health assessments; 3) providing cultural orientation courses and 4) organizing transportation for refugees from the camps in eastern Nepal to their final destination in the United States.

en.full: Harmonization of Protocols for Tuberculosis Diagnosis and Treatment of the Bhutanese Refugees in Nepal (HAPT

en.value: International Organization for Migration (IOM) will work with Association of  Medical Doctors, Asia (AMDA) in seven camps in the south east part of Nepal to  provide tuberculosis (TB) screening and treatment for Bhutanese refugees.  Currently TB screening and treatment protocol implemented in the camps differs  from the protocol of the resettlement countries. The purpose of this project is  to ensure that the refugees who apply for resettlement and those who have not  yet entered resettlement programmes receive the same effective TB diagnosis and  treatment.

en.full: Trafficking Risk Reduction in Nepal (TRRIN)

en.value:
Lack of economic opportunities is one of the major factors driving people to migrate and giving traffickers the opportunity to lure potential victims. In cooperation with the Government of Nepal, NGOs and private sector businesses, IOM provides economic rehabilitation to returned victims and potential victims of trafficking through skills training, job placement and micro-enterprise setup.
NGOs are responsible for psychosocial counseling of the beneficiaries and supporting them in day to day management of their Micro-enterprises. The corporate houses extend business opportunities / franchisees to the beneficiaries and assist them by providing – business specific training, market linkages, skils training and job placements. The Government extends legal and infrastructural support to the initiatives. In addition to the financial inputs IOM is involved in the overall planning and coordination among various stakeholders, including Implementation and monitoring of all the project activities.

en.full: Exploring Livelihood Options for Trafficked Women in Nepal (LOPS)

en.value: To date there has been little research on post trafficking livelihoods or how the issues raised by trafficking intersect with development agendas. IOM in collaboration with Newcastle University, UK and the Non Governmental Organization “Shakti Samuha” is undertaking a research to explore the situation of returnee trafficked women. A key aspect of this research is to gain knowledge that is grounded in the actual experiences of the Nepalese trafficked returnee women themselves and how returnee livelihoods intersect with sexuality and citizenship. Furthermore project facilitates the current debates on the citizenship in the Constitution writing process through ongoing dialogue with relevant subject committees of the Constituent Assembly and Women’s Caucus of the legislative parliament.

en.full: Fairness and Efficiency in Reparations to Conflict-Affected Persons (FERC)

en.value: Over 14,000 people lost their lives and thousands more were the victims of gross human rights violations during the ten-year conflict which began in 1996 and ended with the signing of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement in 2006. IOM Nepal in partnership with OHCHR-Nepal is working with the Ministry of Peace and Reconstruction (MoPR) to develop and implement a comprehensive reparation policy in line with international human rights and humanitarian law standards.  In addition to developing reparations policy, the project will increase the capacity of relevant government agencies including MoPR as well as TRC and COI-D to develop and implement the needed procedures, processes and guidelines including a database essential for the successful implementation of a reparations program.

WFP provides daily food rations to tens of thousands of Bhutanese refugees living in seven camps in eastern Nepal since 1992. In 2011, WFP currently provides food assistance to 70,000 refugees and micronutrient supplementation to refugee children. Additionally, WFP implements supplementary activities such as home gardening, vocational training, HIV/AIDS awareness and loan scheme programmes that aim to endow beneficiaries with practical, life-rebuilding tools and skills for legal employment.

en.full: Save the Children Strategic Framework for Cooperation 2010 -2012

en.value:
Education: The focus of the education program is to reach the most marginalized communities. High priority is given to achieve universal primary education with a focus on gender parity and ensuring access to quality learning opportunities to all with a focus on girls and marginalized groups.

	Child Protection: All vulnerable and survivor children will benefit from advocacy and capacity building of law implementing agencies program conducted at the national level. While the focused program to be implemented in the Mid and Far Western regions will particularly reach to the following children:

	
		30,000 vulnerable children including orphans, Badi, and socially and economically poor;
	
		5,000 survivors of violence;
	
		6,000 conflict affected children; and 5,000 women vulnerable to Chhaupadi. 


	Child rights: The primary beneficiaries of the project are children up to age of 18 years. SCNN ensures that no children are discriminated however; SCNN will focus its target to children who are from most marginalized and disadvantaged population, including promoting girls participation. The secondary target group of this component of the project are:

	 

	
		The Ministry of Women, Children and Social Welfare and the focal points on child rights implementation
	
		The networks for child rights and participation
	
		The child clubs and their networks
	
		The National Human Rights Commission and any other HR monitoring bodies
	
		National Non Governmental Organizations

en.full: Rehalibitation of Critical Trail Bridges

en.value:
The proposed fund shall be utilised to procure the required steel parts including steel decks, anchorage parts, gabion mesh etc. required to rehabilitate the ‘critical’ trail bridges. SDC will procure the materials through a local bidding procedure and hand over the materials to the respective District Development Committees (DDC). The Trail Bridge Support Unit managed by Helvetas shall provide all the required technical and administrative support to SDC.

	 

	Districts are the main implementers at the operational level. Once they receive the steel parts from SDC, they shall allocate adequate budget for labour and other materials such as cement, sand and aggregate. It is also the responsibility of the DDC to organise the contribution from communities wherever applicable. All other approaches concerning social inclusion, transparency and governance, conflict sensitivity, insurance of labour, timely payments, steering, monitoring etc will be applied as usual

en.full: South Asia Food and Nutrition Security Initiative (SAFNSI)

en.value: South Asia Food and Nutrition Security Initiative (SAFANSI) forms part of the Government's commitment to advance Millennium Development Goals (MDG) in South Asia: MDG 1C reduce hunger; MDG 4 reduce child deaths; and MDG 5 improve maternal health. Malnutrition's most devastating impact is on foetal growth, and during the first two years of a child's life. Malnutrition accounts for up to 40% of child deaths each year. Despite healthy levels of economic growth, many of South Asia's countries have persistent and unacceptable levels of malnutrition with complex causality. South Asia has both the highest rates and the largest numbers of malnutrition in the world. Gender inequality and social exclusion are at the heart of the malnutrition problem in South Asia. About 23% (336 million) of the population in South Asia are routinely hungry, without access to enough calories, every day. This is greatly undermining human development and limiting South Asia's productivity with potential GDP loss estimates up to 3%. The funding of this initiative for SAFANSI will be a grant payment to a multi-donor trust fund administered by the World Bank, who will oversee activities to advance MDGs 1c, 4 and 5. The total value of this multi-country initiative is $5.77 million over 3 years, starting 2010-11.

identification of livestock pockets by district Livestock Action Team by using poverty maps of the project districts; development of about 6,900 livestock groups with at least 35% women participation; social mobilization through local NGO's/CBO's ; community level extension by Community Livestock Assistants(CLS); capacity developement of farmer groups, DLS staff, partner NGO's/CBO's and livestock- based enterpreneurs.

Fifteen livestock improvement models identified as suitable for small and resource poor farmers; livestock productivity improvement through intensive forage development, provision of veterinary and breeding services(with emphasis on promotion of private practice), financing through microfinance intermediaries

Improvement and/or establishment of milk market infrastructure (chilling centres) and retail outlets (dairy shops); meat processing marketing infrastructure development(slaughter houses/slabs/meat shops). improvement and/or establishment of live animal market/ market animal collection centres.
D. Project Management Services
A multi-sectoral project interventions for improved livelihood of the project beneficiaries.

Establishment of a central office led by a Project Manager, supported by technical assistance team to support project implementation.

en.full: 61-13104012-KAT (Education) Promoting education for sustainable development with a particular focus on integrating disaster risk reduction and management in the education sector

en.value:
Initial meetings and consultations were held with Nepal National Commission for UNESCO, teacher training centres, curriculum development centres and other key stakeholder in order to prepare modalities to build the capacity of education officials on DRR and its integration in education sector.
	• Participating regularly in Education Cluster Group Meeting on emergency on disaster risk reduction and emergency support response
	• A 2 days' workshop was jointly organized by MOE, UNICEF, SC and UNESCO with the support of UNESCO Bangkok Office on DRR in education sector with a view to reach agreement on a coherent and holistic approach to DRR in the education sector and to explore strategic options for integrating DRR into education sectorial planning, and how partners can support this. 70 participants from MOE, UN agencies, development partners and I/NGOs participated in the workshop. Workshop was facilitated by UNESCO, UNICEF and Nepal Risk reduction consortium's expert
	
	• With the support of NRC secondee a mapping of DRR activities in Nepal's Education Sector has been undertaken and shared during the 2 days joint workshop on DRR in education sector held in January 2012.
	• A flyer on "DRR in Education an imperative for education policymakers" prepared by UNESCO Bangkok has been chosen by education cluster group for its adaption and translation into Nepali language as an advocacy materials.
	
	• Meetings with key stakeholders have contributed to enhance understanding on the importance of DRR in education and bring all key stakeholders on board and work together to build the capacity of education officials on DRR in education including integration of DRR into teacher training and curriculum.
	
	• A 2 days' workshop contributed to enhance understating on DRR in education among education officials and other key stakeholders. The workshop agreed on 10 key actions to be undertaken in next 12 months as road map for DRR in education. • Analysis of mapping and other materials shared during the workshop further contributed in raising the awareness among participants on DRR in education.
	
	• Integrating DRR in education demand huge capacity including conceptual clarity among key stakeholder
	
	• Collaboration with Nepal National commission for UNESCO, MOE, UN agencies contributes brings key stakeholders to work together and also ensures cost effectiveness and sustainability of teh programme.

en.full: Jaladh Integrated Watershed and Natural Resource Management Program

The concept of Open Village School will be established under which 2600 villagers will receive training on eco-literacy, bio-intensive gardening, watershed literacy, livestock management, local history and geography, current affairs, natural pest management, primary health, women’s rights, gender based violence and other topics.
	
		525 people will get orientation on HIV/AIDS, sexual and reproductive health rights, natural resource management, democracy and other topics.
	
		14 different training packages for illiterate people will be developed and distributed.
	
		225 people within the villages will receive training/ develop skills in facilitation, teaching and organisation.
	
		1,650 people will attend meetings and discussions.
	
		Capacity building and infrastructure development will be provided to Jaladh Youth Club. Under the initiative, 950 school youth will receive training/ orientation in ecology, watersheds, history, the global challenges, agro-ecology, family planning, HIV/AIDS and sexual and reproductive health rights.
	
		18 learning resource centres with audio-visual capacities will be established and managed
	
		80 youth (both boys and girls) will receive training and develop skills in facilitation and organisation
	
		470 (other) girls and boys will participate in meetings, village activities, advocacy and campaign work.
	
		About 2699 people will receive Functional Literacy
	
		Approximately three community based organisations and 10 village organisations will be established.
	
		Apart from other regular study tours, information and documentation activities,  the project will establish a 400 m2 of demonstration garden at the Life school center
	
		Under Rural Workers and Crafts People’s Programme (RWCPP) 200 landless will receive training on new technical skills and efforts will be catered towards providing and use rights to 200 others.
	
		144 landless people will receive training/ basic skills in conducting meetings, basic primary health care, trade unions and other issues.
	
		Participatory Conservation and Community Activities Programme (PCCAP) of the project will assist  in preparing 100 village plan/projects
	
		Group Partnership Programme (GPP)  will help form and operationalise 18 cooperatives with lead representation from poor and socially excluded families
	
		35 groups will receive training/ skills to improved their natural resource management capacity
	
		The Whole Watershed Programme (WWP) hopes to ensure access of  100 households to natural resources. This also hopes to conserve and manage 200ha of currently fragile land.
	
		Advocacy and Policy Dialogue Programme (APD) will provide training/orientation on basic advocacy skills to 500 men and women. Similarly, Advocacy campaign will be conducted for popular co-management  of Churia

en.full: Enhancing Mobile Population Access to HIV/AIDs Service, Information & Support (EMPHASIS)

en.value:
Prevention services through establishing linkages with the existing government services in the source, transit and destination locations.
	
		Treatment, care and support through establishing linkages with public and private service providers at source and destination points to ensure continuity of services across the continuum of mobility without interruption
	
		Reducing the vulnerability of mobile women in sex work and wives of mobile men at the source areas
	
		Establishing and strengthening community based organizations, local government and NGO’s to reduce vulnerability of mobile populations
	
		Linking NGOs and CBOs at source, transit and destination through use of appropriate information and communication technology and establishment of a database to connect between mobile populations and their families in source, transit and destination areas
	
		Sensitizing and orienting people with whom mobile populations will come into contact such as transport organizations, highway hoteliers, traders, border security personnel,  customs and other local officials at transit points; improving their ability and effectiveness in advising mobile populations, with a particular focus on the specific vulnerabilities and denial of rights faced by mobile women.
	
		A regional research centre - the project envisages the establishment of a regional research centre on HIV and mobility, managed by The Overseas Development Institute (ODI), which will house all the information and data about mobility and HIV in the region and undertake specific research, surveys and studies on a regular basis to ensure availability and quality of information to support the efforts of evidence based advocacy at national and regional levels
	
		Research studies - will be conducted to better understand the gender dynamics and gender based vulnerabilities of mobile populations and their family members
	
		Monitoring and Evaluation - The project management unit will work with the research centre to monitor and evaluate the project, in order to guarantee that the learning cycle is active and constantly feeds into more effective implementation, resulting in better practice

en.full: Policy assistance for bio-secure agro-food supply chain enhanced market access and food security for the small holding rural sector

en.value:
1.1. Recruitment of national and TCDC consultants

1.2. Conduct National stakeholders’ workshop / meetings

1.3 Review the current situation of level of bio-security in the agro-food supply chain and identify policy and institutional constraints to transform the agro-food supply chain into bio-secure

1.4 Develop a draft on national policy framework and institutional reform        necessary  for  bio-security based on the analysis of economic benefits

1.5. Draft a national food safety and quality policy (to fit within the national policy framework) and develop the action plan for implementation of the same

1.6. Analyze and prepare risk analysis and management frameworks

2.1. Assess the existing situation on the role of public and private sectors on agro-food supply chain and of level of bio-security in the agro-food supply chain covering role of various stakeholders including farmers, producers, processors, transporters, other service providers, retailers, consumers, etc

2.2. Review the cost of compliance with bio-secure requirements (Prepare/design an analytical framework and assist in its implementation in a selected area, in collaboration with the National Consultants, to estimate the cost of adopting bio-secure practices (i.e GAP) by small farmers)

3.1. Conduct a National stakeholders’ workshop / meetings and develop training modules for ToT and subject specific trainings, and their curricula and materials

3.2. Organize a ToT (12- 15 days) and develop Master Trainers (15-20 Participants)

3.3. Carry out various level in-country trainings to the participants of the   public and private sectors on the subject of bio-secure agriculture

3.4. Carry out on the job training for the operation and troubleshooting of HPLC and LCMS to analyze contaminants, residues, additives, etc. in food and feeds in abroad country

3.5. In-country/onsite training on LCMS, GCMS for operation and troubleshooting   on  analysis of contaminants, residues, additives, etc. in food and feed materials by TCDC experts

4.1. Develop standards of the NTIS identified exportable commodities including coffee and dairy products that are in harmony with Codex

4.2. Strengthen laboratory-testing facility for the analysis of contaminants especially heavy metals, pesticides and veterinary drug residues.

4.3. Operationalize CODEX national secretariat for continual standard development as well as establishment and strengthening of National Codex Committees

en.full: Koshi Basin Program Phase 1 (ICIMOD)

en.value: The Intergovernmental Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) initiative provides funding for a 'multi-disciplinary river basin resource management programme' targeting the Koshi River Basin, covering parts of China, Nepal, and India.  The overall goal is to contribute to inclusive poverty reduction and enhanced resilience to climate change by securing and sustaining freshwater ecosystem services. Australia's contribution will: develop a basin wide knowledge based in a web-based information sharing platform; propose options for improved agriculture in different geo-climatic parts of the basin; and provide detailed case studies of the underlying causes and management options for a range of water hazards. Improving the management of the waters of the Himalayan Rivers is critical to improving the livelihood of more than 500 million of the world's poorest people. The total value of this multi-country initiative is $3.0 million over 4 years, starting 2011-12.

en.full: Trial Bridge Sub Sector Programme III

en.value:
Districts are the main implementers at the operational level. It supports the local communities in building their own bridges. As the beneficiaries themselves can best assess the need for a bridge, the communities initiate the bridge demand along with their commitment to mobilise local resources (labour and local materials), plus their willingness to assume responsibilities, prove the feasibility of the venture, and finally they construct a bridge. In this context, a comprehensive bridge demand of over 6000 bridges across the country has been compiled. Every year, according to the budget availability, these are screened and prioritised through a set of criteria such as distance gained, population served (giving higher weightage to DAGs), accidents occurred due to the absence of the bridge. The UC then takes the lead role for the completion of a bridge. For this purpose, an Agreement is established between the concerned UC and the DDC. Transparency is maintained at all stages through various tools like: public hearing/auditing, fact sheets, third party technical audit and participatory decision making process. Only local people are given the opportunity to work on the construction and the maintenance work of trail bridges. Another important aspect is the monitoring to ensure that equal wages are paid for equal work. Efforts are made to ensure that labourers are insured against death and accidents. Formation of an inclusive UC is one of the major tasks to ensure conflict sensitivity. The representation of women in the UCs is aimed at 33% with executive posts provisioned for DAGs in order to help address the needs of the DAG members.

	 

	Trail Bridge SWAp Coordination Committee ("TBSCC") is established as an apex level body comprising representatives of GoN as well as that of all development partners supporting TB SWAp, to give direction/guidance to the implementation of the TB SWAp. DoLIDAR is the executing agency on behalf of GoN and Trail Bridge Support Unit (TBSU)/Helvetas is the TA provider on behalf of SDC. SDC proposes to continue with Helvetas for this final phase (without going into a tendering process), because of their legacy and leading expertise in this field. Infact, SDC would not foresee a next phase without the involvement of Helvetas.

en.value: The Safer Migration (SaMi) project will contribute to decreasing the socio-economic and psychosocial costs by building the migrants’ knowledge about the migration process and their rights and by providing legal and psychosocial support to those who were victimized in the migration process. SaMi aims at increasing the benefits of migration by providing skills trainings for potential migrants especially to people from poor and socially discriminated groups (DAG) of Khotang district. The Government of Nepal together with civil society partners will be supported to identify a strategy to better implement the Foreign Employment Act (FEA).

en.full: TA 7158-NEP: Strengthening Capacity for Management for Development Results

en.value:
Activities with Milestones
 

Output 1: MPPW, MLD, MOES, and NPC implement an MfDR approach in planning, budgeting, and monitoring their mandated responsibilities 
 

1.1  Help establish steering committee, focal points, and groups, by March 2009.
1.2  Review and revise the results frameworks, business plans, and other MfDR initiatives in line with TYIDP and emerging priorities of the Government.
1.3  Support the ministries to integrate their business plans and results frameworks into the planning, budgeting, and monitoring systems, projects, and programs.
1.4 Help NPC to streamline results criteria in its project screening system in close consultation with line ministries and MOF.  
 
Output 2: Results frameworks, indicators, and business plans implemented in MOAC and MOWR operations
 
2.1 Assess status of MfDR practices in the two ministries, including review of their mandates, vision, mission, and goals.
2.2 Help the ministries to develop result frameworks, performance indicators, and business plans in line with the sectoral results framework of the TYIDP and development priorities of the Government, in close consultation with NPC and relevant stakeholders.
2.3 Support the ministries to integrate business plans and results frameworks into the annual planning, budgeting, and monitoring systems, projects, and programs.
 
Output 3: Results-based budgets implemented by two public agencies
 
3.1 Assess the readiness of agencies for RBB using ADB’s MfDR readiness tool.
3.2 Develop RBB modules for two agencies, with performance indicators on delivery of effective and efficient services.
3.3 Support, guide, and monitor the implementation of RBB, and report regularly to MOF and NPC.
3.4 Design and conduct a survey to assess the impact of pilots on service delivery improvements, and organize dissemination programs.
 
Output 4: Capacity of staff in selected agencies to apply MfDR approaches enhanced
 
4.1 Assess MfDR capacity in NPC and pilot ministries and establish baseline data on capacity.
4.2 Specify training needs of institutions (including scope/content of external training), and design capacity-development programs and training materials.
4.3 Organize capacity-development programs for strategic managers and for the operational level, and training-of-trainers programs.
4.4  Undertake training impact assessment and reflect improvements in competency in applying core MfDR skills.

en.full: High Value Agriculture Project (HVAP) in Hills and Mountains Areas

en.value:
In this High Value Agriculture Project in Hills and Mountains of Mid-western Region, funded by IFAD, SNV is responsible for implementation of Component 1 in which it will work together with the Local Capacity Builder Agro-Enterprise Center (AEC). 

    The Component 1 covers selection of companies for contractual production, value chain analysis, selection of producers, baselines and actual signing of contracts between the agribusinesses and the producers. 
    SNV also provides advisory services to Component 2 which provides the necessary support to the intended value chain development: formation/strengthening value chain producers groups, initiatives to promote gender and social inclusion, support for high value commodity production and post-harvest activities, establishment of a grant-based value chain development fund, and support for district operations and inclusion of remote communities. SNV has a small implementation role in Component 2 to promote gender and social within the project and among project stakeholders and contracted implementers. 
    Component 3 provides for project management and linked activities including M&E and knowledge management. Next to providing advisory services to Component 3, SNV is also responsible for the implementation of its knowledge management component.

en.full: Building statistical capacity for quality food security and nutrition information in support of better informed policies

en.value:
Activity 1.1:  Inception mission to set up the country’s multisectoral taskforce for discussing and planning the activities of both FBS and NHS in line with their terms of reference.

Activity 1.2: Regional workshop (of five days on the FAO methodological framework of preparing the supply and utilization accounts (SUA) for compiling the FBS for representatives of MoA and NSO of  participating countries.

Activity 1.3: Representatives of MoA of each country will prepare the SUA for the past four years based on the available agricultural and food data and compile the yearly FBS.

Activity 1.4: National workshop among the members of the country multisectoral taskforce to identify and to assess the progress in preparation of the SUA.

Activity 2.1: Country’s NSO staff  prepare the required data files on food consumption derived from the NHS as per FAO data files instructions. 

 Activity 2.2: Country’s NSO staff, together with the support of nutritionist from Ministry of Health, prepare the Food Composition Table of nutrients conversion factors which are essential for both updating the inputs of the SUA and for deriving FSNS.

Activity 2.3: Regional workshop of five days on the FAO methodological framework of deriving food security and nutrition statistics from the NHES for representatives of NSO and MoA of participating countries.

Activity 2.4:  Country’s NSO staff draft the food security analysis based on the results derived from the NHS in the regional workshop.

Activity 2.5: Institutional structure and the capacity of concerned departments/institutions which are engaged in nutrition statistical data collection and analysis, and their inter-linkages reviewed and technical advice provided with an aim to strengthen the institutional capacity and promote inter-ministerial/departmental coordination.

Activity 3.1: A five day National Writeshop among all representatives of the different national institutions constituting the country’s multisectoral taskforce to analyse and interpret the FBS and FSNS for the write up of the Country flagship technical “Food Security and Nutrition Status” report.

Activity 3.2:  The multisectoral taskforce finalizes the Country flagship technical “Food Security and Nutrition Status” report  within one month after the writeshop with the technical backstopping assistance of the food security analysis consultant.

Activity 3.3: Check and edit of the country flagship technical “Food Security and Nutrition Status” report by Food Security Analysis consultant and FAORAP .

Activity 3.4: National Seminar for the presentation and discussion of the country flagship technical “Food Security and Nutrition Status” by the multisectoral taskforce.

Activity 3.5:  Printing of 250 copies of the country flagship technical report, “Food Security and Nutrition Status” for dissemination.

Activity 3.6: A three day Regional Workshop will be held among representatives of the participating countries coming from the NSO, MoA and the Multisectoral taskforce coordinator for presenting countries’ results, findings and recommendations.

en.full: Supporting Investments in Water Security in River Basins

en.value:
This is a Regional TA funded by Asian Development Bank for Indonesia, Nepal and Uzbekistan. Estimated cost of TA is US$ 2.43 million of which US$ 2.00 million will  be financed by ADB on a grant basis from Japan special Fund. JWA (Japan Water Agency) will  contribute US$ 0.43 million equivalent through in-kind support. It has two components:
I. Preparation for future water resources management programs that combine structuralo and non-structural investments to increase water security in three pilot basin areas and to improve exiting river basin management plans.
II. In-country  and regional capacity development activities to prepare government agencies, river basin organizations and other stakeholders for these future investment programs, including demonstrating activities to start implementating innovative approaches to increase water securitiy in the three basins.
In the case of Nepal, the TA will help to identify investment needs in  preparation for future feasibility studies for projects to increase  water security in the pilot river basins of Bagmati.

en.full: Towards Achieving the Elimination of the Worst Forms of Child Labour as Priority (ACHIEVE)

en.value:
- Review the report and data of the 2010 Child Labour Survey and prepare estimates to identify areas of high concentration of hazardous child labour at the district level.

	- Prepare a District Mainstreaming Strategy in a from of a briefing note and identify key entry points in the various plans and frameworks (including those related to the economic and social empowerment of the families).

	- Identify most feasible monitoring and reporting mechanisms to integrate child labour issue, particularly those linked with district/national planning mechanisms.

	-  Prepare a simple and low-cost ‘how-to’ manual (including tools and estimations) to serve as guidance for replication/adaptation of the model by other districts/sub-districts.

	- Identify the most appropriate survey for purposes of identifying the number of children in the worst forms of child labour, age-group, gender, socio-economic status of the family, education status, workplaces where children are working including mapping of services and service providers  for referrals and mainstreaming purpose. 

	- Develop social mobilization strategy to bring community members (including community leaders, families, school teachers, hospitals, youth, human rights groups and children among others) on-board.

	- Through involvement of social partners, seek participation of employers and workers and their groups in programs, campaigns and referral processes in the two districts to ensure that children of legal working age are protected and those below working age are not involved in the worst forms or hazardous forms of child labour.

	- Identify and facilitate linkages through joint programmes with schools, training and other services in cooperation with the DWCB and Child Protection/Welfare Committees

	- Organize ToT for 50 national trainers using the Capacity Development Training Module prepared under Child Labour Phase I Project in cooperation with the MoLE/CLERS.

en.full: Nepal Energy Efficiency Programme (NEEP)/Support to Energy Efficiency

en.value:
Component 1:Policy Support
Major activities
·      Provide information on international good practice for strategy design, policy and implementation Programs
·      Support and facilitate selected stakeholder consultation to enable a structured stakeholder-policy dialogue
·      Support the formulation of a biomass energy strategy(BEST) including identification of industrial use of biomass and agricultural residues as part of or complementary to the overall energy strategy
·      Provide information and support for initiatives aiming at the introduction of energy efficiency issues and targets into the next 3 year development plans
·      Support intermediaries to create public awareness on energy conservation groups issues
Component 2: Energy Efficiency in Households
This component has two subcomponents.
A.    To reduce the specific electricity consumption of grid connected households
B.     To reduce the biomass consumption of rural households
Major activities for subcomponent 2A
·       Provide information on international good practice on minimum standards and energy efficiency labeling for electric household appliances
·       Study financial benefits and burdens on consumer and utility side on basis of drafted minimum standards. The study will also analyse the conditions in isolated electricity grids.
·       If required support NBSM to devise minimum standards and labeling for household appliances
·       Support awareness raising for households and capacity building for institutions implementing and enforcing the mandatory minimum standards 
Major activities for subcomponent 2B
·       Support a study to conceptualize the accelerated dissemination of improved efficient cooking stoves. The study takes socioeconomic, gender and cultural aspects of the target groups into account.
·       Support management, implementation and monitoring of scaling up programmes under AEPC.
Component 3:Energy Efficiency in Industry
Major activities: It is envisaged that relevant private sector institutions found and operate an Energy Efficiency centre. The centre shall operate and provide services on commercial principles while being supported to perform the following activities
·      Training of energy auditors and energy managers
·      Capacity development of chambers of Industry and the financial sector

en.full: RRI – Recovery and Reconstruction initiative
Mediating Local Conflict and Reducing Vulnerability Post Earthquake Recovery (Nepal)

en.value: The Conflict Mediation in Post Earthquake Recovery supports Nepal's long term recovery following the devastating earthquake on 25 April 2015. The early recovery package of support will focus on three key themes: meeting the educational needs of vulnerable children, with a focus on girls and children with disabilities, as they transition back to school and “building back better” ; rebuilding livelihoods of women and other vulnerable populations; and rebuilding social cohesion, by ensuring there is access to alternative dispute resolution for addressing disaster-related conflict, violence and exploitation of women. Within the early recovery package, Australia provided funds to the Asia Foundation (TAF) in Nepal for a program to address conflicts and vulnerabilities related to earthquake recovery and assistance in Nepal. The program will address, in particular, disputes related to identity, resettlement, land and resource use, and gender-based violence (GBV). The program will support facilitated dialogue, and community mediation in order to create and sustain an enabling environment for effective earthquake recovery efforts. The total value of this investment is $3.0 million over 2 years, starting May 2015.

en.value: The two earthquakes of 25 April and 12 May 2015, have heavily affected the monuments and temples within the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage property, as well as many other cultural sites in the north western area of Nepal. UNESCO has been assigned by the government a coordination role for all cultural heritage rehabilitation projects. This concerns assessment of damage, inventorying, documentation, capacity building of national experts, emergency consolidation, restoration and rebuilding of historical structures and fundraising efforts. It is a key challenge to reach a common understanding to improve seismic resilience, maintaining the values and  finding appropriate approaches for reconstruction (whether using traditional construction methods and/ or integrating modern reversible technologies). In this context, the Kathmandu Office will continue its coordinating role and garner international support. It will support Nepal’s Department of Archaeology (DoA) in the rehabilitation and reconstruction of the heritage sites through implementing multiple extra-budgetary projects with participation of various national, international and local stakeholders.

en.full: Budget Analysis and Public Finance Management assessment of Ministries involved in the implementation of the Agriculture Development Strategy of Nepal CTR 380651
549NEP5000 (CI) - Empowering people to enjoy their Right to Information for greater accountability of Nepal's power holders

en.value:
1.2.3. Describe and define the target groups and final beneficiaries, their needs and constraints and how the action will address these needs
	
	Target groups:
	The three main target groups are journalists, local "change agents" (teachers, lawyers and civil society activists) and government officials.
	The 250 journalists to be selected to participate in the training provided by the project come from the areas mostly affected by press freedom violations. These incidents have been, since 2007, most intense in Nepal's central plains and the eastern hills. Therefore, while journalists in the capital and urban centres have been largely secure, those working in the plains in general and in the eastern hills have been attacked, threatened, or continuously harassed by different interest groups, many of which are also armed. Therefore this project will focus mainly on these areas, where, according to FNJ estimates, there are around 1,500 journalists in the eastern region and around 1,500 to 2,000 journalists in the central plains. These are the areas where working as a journalist is most dangerous, and where the journalists need most support in building their capacity both in investigative journalism and personal safety. Many of these journalists have not had any training in journalism, and do not understand their possibilities and responsibilities in serving the public with accurate, non-partisan information. Therefore through building their capacity, we can improve the access to information for people on district level. The journalists will be selected in cooperation with the local chapters of Federation of Nepali journalists, ensuring equal representation of women, lower castes and other marginalized groups. A special focus will be given to journalists who have already made attempts to practice investigative journalism, but who do not necessarily have the necessary skills yet.
	The 250 local mediators (teachers, lawyers and civil society activists, depending on the area) are people who are active in their community and to whom people come to ask for help. These mediators will be trained as local focal points to raise awareness on the RTI Act and its relevance locally as well as for helping local people with their information requests to the government offices. In order to increase the synergies between project components the local mediators will be selected from the same areas as the journalists. That way the journalists and mediators can support each other's work.
	The third target group of the project are government officials who are responsible for the implementation of the Right to Information law. Many government offices have information officers, but in many cases their capacity remains low. By organizing local level orientation sessions for the government information officers the project seeks to build their capacity and to orient them to their public service task. In addition, through linking the trained journalists and mediators to these sessions, the project aims at building local level multi-stakeholder networks that on a local level work jointly to increase and improve people's access to public information.
	
	The project mainstreams gender throughout all its activities. In addition, the project will ensure women's equal participation in all training programmes. Individual women will be identified and encouraged to apply, and the trainings will be organized in a manner that suits the time constraints of women.
	It is much more challenging for a woman to step up and speak for herself because of the cultural and social norms of gender in Nepal, let alone to demand for information from government officials who often are men. In addition, a woman is likely to be treated differently from a man if she approaches a government office and requests for information. This specific approach will be emphasized in the training of local mediators, so that they will be able to offer locally-relevant solutions - e.g. cooperating with local women's groups, where the information request does not come from an individual woman but a group of women could help ease the social challenges. In addition, the issue of gender equality and women's specific needs will be addressed also in the orientation given to government officials.
	The gender equality aspect will also be covered in the handbook for journalists and the handbook for local mediators, both to be published in the course of the project. In addition, the project will ensure all promotional products, such as posters or leaflets, go through a gender analysis, ensuring the material is also suitable for women and doesn't support gender stereotypes.
	
	The overall objective of this action is to improve the transparency of Nepal's government and the accountability of decision-making through a broader implementation of the Right to Information Act. The action also has three specific objectives: 1) Citizens have access to information that is relevant to them and are hence motivated to exercise their democratic rights; 2) Journalists recognize their role as the watchdogs of the power holders and proactively seek and publish correct and timely information and 3) Local level government officials understand their role as public servants and are more willing to share public information.
	
	Activity group 1: Building the capacity of journalists on investigative journalism / RTI / personal safety
	The activities of this group include training of trainers with an international trainer, training of 250 journalists on RTI and safety, a handbook for journalists on RTI and a fellowship programme and competition for best investigative journalism using RTI Law
	Output: Journalists have the capacity to use RTI in investigative journalism and to protect themselves while using it.
	Result: Journalists are actively using RTI for the purposes of investigative journalism and simultaneously protect their personal safety.
	
	Activity group 2: Raising public awareness on right to information and how to use the RTI Law
	The activities of this group include public awareness campaigning, network of local "mediators" and a handbook and advocacy material for local communities on how to use the RTI Law for obtaining locally relevant information
	Output: People have the knowledge of their constitutionally protected right to information and of the importance of the RTI Law to their lives as well as of how to submit requests for information.
	Result: People actively utilize the RTI Law by making information requests to relevant public agencies.
	
	Activity group 3: Improving the general climate for the successful implementation of the RTI Law
	The activities of this group include local meetings with journalists and government information officers, high-level seminar on the implementation of the RTI act and establishing a loose network of civil society organizations and other potential stakeholders promoting RTI
	Output: Power holders understand the possibilities and limitations of the RTI act and their role in its implementation
	Result: Journalists, civil society activists and local mediators jointly work towards ensuring open and transparent society where public information is shared freely and without problems.

en.value:
The project focuses on empowerment of poor vulnerable and socially excluded women in 3 districts of Churia as well as building capacity of partner NGOs to promote sustainable socio-economic change for these women.



	The project will be implemented through a national network called Himalayan Grassroots Women's Association for Natural Resource Management in Nepal (HIMWANTI) and three district level NGOs


	Forum for Social Development (INDRENI), Nepal Rural Self-Reliance Campaign (NRUSEC) and Nari Ship Shrijana Kendra (NSSK).



	The project will reach 7,500 poor vulnerable socially excluded women and their families and community based organizations, natural resource management groups, mothers groups, government line agencies and womenâ€™s networks at local and national.



	The Project's major activities are:


	- Awareness raising and empowerment of PVSE women to access natural management resources


	- Identification and usage of income generating opportunities


	- On-farm and off-farm training, vocational training


	- Awareness raising on gender based violence and reproductive health


	- Training on disaster risk reduction, development of emergency plans and small scale mitigation measures


	- Capacity building of local partner NGOs and local resource.

en.value:
Brief introduction of project location containing geographical, economical, demographic, educational, health service, environment, and public infrastructure related information.


 

Kathmandu District

 

Kathmandu District is a district located in Kathmandu Valley, Province No. 3 of Nepal, a landlocked country in South Asia. It is one of the 75 districts of Nepal, covers an area of 395 km2 (153 sq mi), and is the most densely populated district of Nepal with 1,744,240 in 2011. The district's headquarters is Kathmandu Metropolitan City, also the capital of Nepal. Kathmandu district is one of the three districts located in Kathmandu Valley, which itself is located in the hills of Bagmati Zone, Central Development Region, Nepal. The district is located from 27°27′E to 27°49′E longitude and 85°10′N to 85°32′N latitude.

The people of the district are primarily Newars (Source: Census Report 2011 & District Profile, Kathmandu DDC).

 

As per the recommendation of DCC/DDRC, DCA has chosen the following two locations for project execution.

Bhaktapur district is located in the eastern part of Kathmandu valley, is the smallest among the seventy-five districts of Nepal. It is part of Province No. 3. 5.2.2 Need analysis containing problem tree related to proposed project and need identification process 

 

The assessment for this action was undertaken during the period 15 December 2016 to 16 January 2017. More specifically, the field assessments were done on the following dates:

22 - 24 December 2016: Rapid Assessment through field visits to Shankharapur, Mahalaxmi, Karyabinayak and Mahamanjushree-Nagarkot (current Changunarayan) Municipalities and short qualitative interviews with private sector representatives

2 - 3 January 2017: Focal group and individual interviews at Shankharapur Municipality.

4 January 2017: Focal group and individual interviews in Nagarkot Municipality.

15 January 2017: Observation of Earthquake Safety day and interviews in Shankharapur Municipality mainly with private sector representatives (local cement blocks producers, rice mill owners, construction materials suppliers).

16 January 2017: Meetings and interviews with Nagarkot Naldum Tourism Management Committee, Homestay Association and with CBOs - Friends Help Groups.

The Needs assessment used mainly qualitative methods and information sources to identify the key issues and needs for the two selected municipalities. Analysing the collective experience of the consortium partners, DCA-ADRA-VSO served as the initial foundation of the formulation (ToRs) of the assessment. To avoid bias, the consortium employed an external consultant with extensive experience on Disaster Risk Management in Nepal and abroad to lead the Needs Assessment.  Initially a rapid assessment was conducted in four municipalities in Kathmandu Valley namely Mahamanjushree-Nagarkot, Mahalaxmisthan, Shankharapur and Karyabinayak Municipalities. The selection of these municipalities for the initial study was due to the presence of the consortium partners in these municipalities. The assessment included an initial disaster risk assessment and a need assessment for all the four municipalities. This involved physical observation and random interviews with local communities, private entities and the local authorities. Based on the findings from the four municipalities, two were selected for comprehensive disaster risk and needs assessment namely Mahamanjushree-Nagarkot Municipality (Current Changunarayan) from Bhaktapur District and Shankharapur Municipality in Kathmandu District.

 

Focal group discussions and individual interviews were then carried out with local authority and community representatives in each of the two municipalities including DDCs (current DCCs), District Administration Offices (DAO), Civil Society Organisations (CSOs), CBOs and NGOs working on disaster management and other development programmes. The assessment team also participated in the periodic District Disaster Relief Committee (DDRC) meetings. Consultation meetings (focus discussions) were carried out with selected private sector entities from both the municipalities. These included Nagarkot-Naldum Tourism Development Committee, National Home Stay Association in Nagarkot, and representatives from construction materials suppliers such as self-locking cement block manufacturers, timber suppliers, and food grain processing factories including rice mills, lentil mills, and a private hospital in Shankharapur.

 

Additionally, consultations were done with the representatives from Ministry of Urban Development (MoUD), National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC), and Municipal Association of Nepal (MUAN). Secondary data and information, such as case studies, research publications and policies were reviewed as a part of needs assessment. The material included the National Strategy for Resilient Urban Settlements, Nepal National Report -Third United Nations Conference on Housing and Sustainable Urban Development (Habitat III), study report conducted by Tribhuwan University on Earthquake Damage Assessment in the Traditional Town of Shankharapur and study report conducted by local partner NDRC on the impact of earthquake on elderly, People with Disability (PWDs) and how gender and ethnicity factor into the impact.

 

In the initial four municipalities assessed, a number of common problems were observed. These included (i) limited understanding of municipal authorities and local communities on disaster risk, (ii) limited understanding on exposure, hazards and vulnerability, including minimal information on emergency response and (iii) no platform for availing risk information. For example, authorities have documented neither information nor lessons from the 2015 earthquake response, and various level of impacts based on gender and age. Four areas of risk were identified in both the municipality: (1) Limited knowledge of information management system, as both municipalities lack hazard and exposure information, which could have been used for DRR related planning and execution. 2) Limited institutional governance to manage risk as both municipalities do not have LDRMPs nor abilities to incorporate associated risk information 3) Role of private sector is not recognized in development and execution of municipal plans. Despite substantial contribution to the 2015 earthquake response, the role of private sector has still not officially been recognised. 4) Limited capacity for Emergency Response, with Municipal authorities, community groups and private enterprises lacking proper emergency equipment (no stock keeping) and capacity to use this in an emergency response resulted into delayed response. Supply and maintenance of stock of SAR and life-saving materials is limited and lack of knowledge result in the limited use of material that are already available.

 

The proposed action aims to build the resilience of the Changunarayan and Shankharapur Municipalities through a holistic capacity enhancement approach, integrating local authorities, private sector and the most vulnerable local communities.

 

5.2.3 Linkage of project with national and sectoral policies of the Government of Nepal 

DCA and IPs will coordinate with the municipality offices and other stakeholders working in the districts. The main purpose will be to coordinate with their ongoing and forthcoming development programs and project s with a view to avoiding duplication. The IPs will invite their representatives to participate in planning, implementation and review workshops at district level. They will also invite representative of concerned government district based development and administrative offices and authorities to visit the project community and to provide feedback for improving project implementation as necessary. Each IP at their district will coordinate with their respective district authority to build synergy in their ongoing programs and sustaining the lessons learnt of the project.

 


	Compliance the project activities with the national priority 


This project has been designed with government policy, strategy and programs to provide support to the disaster vulnerable communities in the proposed districts. So, this project is in line with the national priority of government of Nepal to provide support and prepare them for future disaster.

 


	Proportional balance between hardware and software. 


The action will provide disaster preparedness and rescue equipment, establish well equipped Disaster Risk Reduction Information Centre in the both municipalities, establish well equipped learning centers, emergency desk. Under these actions, the project will support physical infrastructure along with technical support. The action will also provide Mason training in both municipalities, Light Search and Rescue Equipment including rope, life jacket, shovels, helmets among others, first aid equipment for both Municipalities. The action will have Municipality Disaster Risk Management Plan (MDRMP), Disaster Risk Sensitive Tourism Development Plan, Risk sensitive contingency/emergency response plan of private hospital and small and medium scale enterprises, Municipality Emergency Preparedness and Response Plan, Household level DRM Plan at community homestay (MEPRP), Business contingency/emergency response plan of tourism industry (hotel/homestay) and District Disaster and Preparedness Plan in hand by the end of this project. In addition to this the action will also support to strengthen the knowledge of government authorities on information management and engage private sectors acknowledging their contribution for post disaster response. A total of 21,274 individuals (of 4579 households) from 5 wards in two municipalities will directly benefit from the action interventions, while 81,000 individuals (total population of two municipalities) will benefit indirectly.

 

5.3       Objectives and Activities with physical targets:

The main objective of the project is to increase preparedness and response capacities of local authorities and communities collaborating with the private sector contributing to the creation of resilient urban municipalities.

en.full: UN Joint  programme of support to LGCDP

en.value:
Empowering communities and community organisations to participate in local governance

	  UNDP will draw on its more than ten years of experience of mobilising local communities to help citizens and communities engage more actively with local governments and for them to hold local governments to account. An important activity will be developing a mechanism for local bodies to systematically involve communities in planning and implementing programmes.



	Enabling local body capacity building

	  The Ministry of Local Development will be assisted to establish and implement a system for building up the capacity of local bodies to provide basic services inclusively and equitably. Two key support areas will be enabling DDCs to better backstop and mentor VDCs, and funding training programmes for local governments, community organisations, user groups and other service delivery agencies. These programmes will emphasise gender sensitivity and social inclusiveness and enable Nepal's 3,915 VDCs to make the best use of the grants of 1.5 million rupees plus ($20,000) they receive each year.



	Enabling central government and national NGOs to support local governments

	  UNDP, UNICEF, UNFPA, and UNCDF will work together to strengthen the policy and national institutional framework for decentralisation, devolution and community development. This will include strengthening the capacity of the Ministry of Local Development to facilitate sector-wise devolution, to design and use a local government performance monitoring system and to mainstream gender equality and social inclusion issues into decentralisation processes. Other key tasks are to support the implementation of the national capacity building strategy for local bodies and to support the three local government associations (ADDCN, MuAN, NAVIN) to work on behalf of their member DDCs, VDCs and municipalities.

en.full: NPL DFID Technical Assistance for Strengthening NewBorn Care Programme
Managing Risk through Economic Development (MRED)

en.value:
To develop an effective and sustainable model of disaster risk reduction (DRR) in vulnerable communities of Nepal. This model will use hazard assessments, including climate modeling, to provide 3,000 households with a more sustainable DRR approach directly linked to their livelihoods, thereby mitigating the human and economic toll of natural disasters on their communities.
	
		Mobilization of gender/ ethnically-balanced DMCs through a concentrated process that focuses on those aspects of traditional DRR programming that have demonstrated potential for sustainability post-intervention.
	
		Training of DMCs in durable and sustainable techniques for mitigation, preparedness, response, and (if relevant) early warning.
	
		Participatory vulnerability and capacity assessments (VCAs) carried out by DMCs with communities and local government that provide an evidence-based platform for selection of DRR activities.
	
		Collaboration with climate expertise set up to a) assess long-term viability of proposed DRR activities, and b) determine if further risks need to be anticipated beyond those identified as priorities in the short-term.
	
		Plant and crop product and services assessments (for bioengineering, improved land/ watershed management and other complementary approaches).
	
		Local market assessments – tenure, high-demand/ high-value commodities cross-referenced with the plant/ crop species assessed for bioengineering, land/ watershed management and improved resiliency.
	
		Engage local and sub-national governments and private sector actors with community/DMC representatives in community selection, vulnerability and market assessments, and subsequent resource mobilization and decision-making.
	
		Facilitated planning of required risk mitigation measures and landscape-scale interventions.
	
		Assess land ownership/ usage patterns of marginal lands and determine target households accordingly.
	
		Train community groupsin protection and mitigation techniques and in the cultivation of disaster mitigating crops with strong income potential.
	
		Implement planned mitigation measures (based on plant/crop species identified under Outcome 1), including cultivation of crops that contribute to chronic disaster mitigation, through bioengineering or improved land/ water management (based on market and technical assessments).
	
		Train farmersin better seed varieties, improved planting techniques, new crops that are more resilient to local hazards.
	
		Link local input suppliers, extension actors and other training entities to ensure sustainability of the services.
	
		Establish maintenance plans for each mitigation measure, and where feasible, linked to economic opportunities from crops/products generated via these mitigation measures.
	
		Support micro and small enterprises, as necessary, for local value addition prior to sales, or for aggregation/ collective marketing and sales.
	
		Farmers, water and forest users and other localgroups formed, as necessary, to reinforce good technical practices and enhance market linkages/ economies of scale.
	
		Based on assessment findings and implementation experience, information regarding plant and crop species suitable for disaster mitigation and income generation compiled into at least two resource manuals in local languages and English for use by local government officials, other communities and partner agencies interested in replication.

en.full: Nepal Flood Response - Humanitarian Assistance

en.value: Funding under this investment represents Australia's support to Nepal in response to the recent devastating floods and landslides that have left over 1.7 million people in need of assistance. Flooding caused by heavy monsoon rains has resulted in over 150 deaths, damaged 65,000 homes and destroyed 64,000 hectares of standing crops across Nepal. Through this investment Australia will provide $2 million to the international relief effort, including $1 million through our humanitarian partnership with Australian non-government organisations and $1 million through the World Food Programme. The assistance will deliver emergency shelter, food, clean water and healthcare for those who have been affected by this disaster. Our contribution to the World Food Programme will enable it to treat 5,900 children under the age of five and 1,600 pregnant and nursing mothers for moderate acute malnutrition in the worst affected areas. In addition to this support, Australia is providing essential hygiene supplies and vital health services to 6,600 women and girls.

This PRRO 200152  aims to provide safety net for 1.2 million food-insecure populations in the Mid/Far West Hill and Mountain Regions of Nepal as well as improve nutritional status among vulnerable children aged 5-69 months.   The operation adopts a food and/or cash-for-assets modality, providing rice and pulses and-or cash to beneficiaries working on building critical community assets, enhancing agricultural productivity and adopting alternative livelihood means.

en.full: Recovery and Rehabilitation of Cultural Heritage in the Kathmandu Valley, Nepal

en.value: The project aims at rehabilitating the monuments and sites of the Kathmandu Valley World Heritage property that suffered extensive damage by the 2015 earthquakes in Nepal. By working with the Department of Archaeology, local communities, employing and training volunteers and building basic infrastructures, site and monuments will be protected from the looting and further destruction. Priority interventions include: sensitive removal of debris, emergency consolidation of monuments at risk of collapse and rehabilitation of livelihood in order to rebuild the cultural tourism potential (on-site restoration work as key tourists' attraction) and generate employment.

en.full: Public Financial Management Support Multi-Donor Trust Fund Contribution (Nepal) - Phase 2

en.value: The objective of the MDTF is to strengthen the performance, transparency and accountability in public financial management in Nepal. The Key Results expected from the projects to be funded through the MDTF are: 1.	Improved  resource management as a result of strengthened PFM systems and processes,2.	Increased awareness and oversight of government PFM processes by diverse constituencies , 3.	Better knowledge of value for money challenges and PFM governance gaps, contributing to improved design of PFM interventions at the country and sector level.The trust fund PDO will be attained through implementation of various sub-projects designed and implemented with support from the MDTF.  The MDTF will be used as a vehicle to support a wide range of activities based on priorities set by the government and development partners broadly categorized under three broad dimensions:  Supply, Demand and Knowledge.  The MDTF will support activities that will:  (a) strengthen the PFM systems and processes (the supply side); (b) strengthen institutions of accountability and civil society to enhance their oversight of PFM processes and performance (the demand side); and (c) deepen knowledge about current PFM practices and options for improvement.

en.value: The Cultural Heritage Preservation Group will be following the traditional practice and using traditional materials to bring the temple back to its original size and shape.  As no drawings exist the reproduction of the temple will be made as authentic as possible based on the surviving historical photos, water color sketches and the original components of the temple. The reconstruction design of the temple will be based on the existing base in stone which will provide the ground floor plan with exact locations of the 20 timber columns. en.full: Support to Transitional Justice efforts in Nepal

en.value: ICTJ: The objective of the project is to work toward that transitional justice mechanisms in Nepal are designed and implemented in a way that is consistent with international best practice, thereby making a significant contribution to peace, justice and reconciliation. Through the project, ICTJ implements a number og activities that support the Nepal Government to pass truth-seeking bills that are in accordance with international standards and best practice; contribute to increased understanding amongst key stakeholders of the roles and relationship between the truth and reconciliation commission (TRC), disappearance commission (DC) and the courts; enable victims of conflict-related crimes and gross human rights violations to receive reparations in accordance with international standards; and, enable victims to effectively participate in all transitional justice mechanisms. RNE has previously funded and worked with ICTJ since 2007 and are of the opinion that ICTJ fulfil their obligations according to the targets of the proposals goal and targets.

en.full: Support to discharge of disqualified maois combattans

en.value: According to the Comprehensive Peace Agreement (CPA) the disqualified Maoist combatants shall be discharged and rehabilitated into society. These 4008 individuals were disqualified through the UNMIN led verification process because they were either under the age of 18 at the date of the peace accord or they were recruited to the Maoist army after this date. The primary objective of this project is to have as many of the VMLRs as possible involved in gainful employment or livelihood opportunities. To achieve this, the project is framed around two complimentary outcomes: 1) VMLRs were supported in their socio-economic rehabilitation; and2) Communities were engaged in supporting the rehabilitation of VMLR participants.
