en.full: Okhaldhunga Recovery and Resilience Program

en.value: Initiate outreach to communities immediately to address high rates of non-compliance and provide basic information about construction standards that will need to be met.Similarly, initial outreach to communities will look to address reasons related with HHs not starting reconstruction in close collaboration with CRCs.Identify and contract technical resource organization(s), institutes or technical persons to deliver technical support in project activities like both the skilled and unskilled mason trainings, construction of low cost model houses, IEC material development etc and involve local contractors (who oversee and direct gangs of laborers and masons in the construction of homes).Provide top-up support and targeted technical assistance to extremely vulnerable households who need in kick-starting the construction or rehabilitation of their homes. This may be applied as financial support (cash transfer) and/or material transport or at one of the five construction stages including, for example, demolishing their damaged homes and removing rubble.Build low cost model houses (one per ward and 65 in total) through vocation and on-the-job mason training. The low-cost model houses will be built for the most vulnerable household in the ward. CRS will adopt the vulnerability criteria developed by NRA for the selection of model house beneficiary. Series of consultation meetings will be held with communities, ward citizen forums and Gaon Palika leadership to ensure that most eligible model house beneficiary is selected through a very transparent process. Upon completion of the model house, the property will be handed over to the beneficiary.CRS will use Central Level Project Implementation Unit (CLPIU) approved model house designs including Stone Masonry Mud Mortar (SMM), SMM with attic roof and RCC for CRS Gorkha Program approved on 09 August 2017. CRS will positively adopt any other models that have been approved by NRA or CLPIU by the time implementation is started.CRS will engage a technical agency to ensure that the low-cost model houses are constructed in a short span of time considering the housing needs of the most vulnerable households. Strong technical oversight from the technical agency through experienced human resources will help in high quality structures. The construction firm will also be engaged in conducting trainings for masons. CRS implementing partners and the construction firm will work in close coordination to ensure that the social mobilization aspects of model house construction and mason training is adequately integrated.CRS will adopt “mobile masons” approach to ensure that house owners and workers involved in construction get adequate on-site technical support through direct supervision. Such support will ensure that the houses built are in compliant with NRA norms. Through this mechanism CRS will engage skilled and unskilled masons to support families and labor working at the household level.  Each mason will be expected to visit every household at each of the 5 key stages of construction:  layout, foundation, wall, roof and fixations (doors and windows) to verify that the house meets guidelines for earthquake resistance.Work closely with its key implementing partners on all community mobilization activities, including outreach to individual families with key information about the GoN processes and EQ-safety measures; animation and capacity development of pre-existing community management structures (whether the CRC or other); identification of extremely vulnerable households in need of specialized assistance; as well as monitoring of all key project activities. To facilitate this process in the field, CRS will depute 11 social mobilization officers through the project.Coordinate with key stakeholders at the district and VDC levels with a concern for working closely with NRA engineers who oversee, review and approve household construction.While starting the project, CRS will conduct a quick assessment to understand the most updated needs and trends in the communities around capacity building of households in general and masons in specific regarding reconstruction of their houses. If majority of the masons has already received training and supply for the skilled labor has increased through Unskilled Labor Training (Vocational training masonry) by other NGOs, CRS will focus on the information, promotion and capacity building for retrofitting techniques. This may require changing some of the key activities and indicators in the Objective 1 for which detailed amendment with scale and scope of the activity targets will be shared with NRA accordingly. The refresher trainings will also include correction manual/retrofitting which will help masons adhere to EQ resistant construction techniques in case of already constructed houses.On-the-job training on retrofitting will include demonstration of such techniques in existing houses. CRS will conduct detailed technical assessments for identifying appropriate retrofitting techniques for different conditions in coordination with local NRA engineers.For the skilled and unskilled mason trainings CRS will prioritize identification of participants from local communities. However, recognizing the fact that significant number of masons/construction workers from terai and other regions of the country are engaged in reconstruction work, CRS will facilitate their participation in mason trainings wherever possible. Series of orientation meetings will be held at the community level for selection of training beneficiaries. In order to encourage participation of needy and motivated women members, CRS will hold orientation meetings with existing women savings/mothers’ groups to ensure that accurate information about the mason trainings is available to women members for them to take an informed decision about participating in trainings.

en.full: 467GLO1007.26 (ED) - CAP EFA: Capacity Assessment for Non-formal Education in Nepal

en.value: According to GMR 2011, Nepal has illiterate population of 7.6 million (or 42% of the total) of whom 67 percent are women. Literacy rates vary by ecological regions with the Hills with highest literacy rate (55%) and the Mountains with the lowest (41%). However, the Terai has the highest number of illiterates followed by the Hills. Large disparities exist between male and female literacy rates in all age groups. According to the 2001 census, the literacy rate for six years and older males (66%) is 23 percentage points higher than that for the same age group of females (43%). The youth literacy rate (15 to 24 years) of 70 percent is significantly higher than the adult literacy rate (age 15 years and above) of 48 percent The weak capacity in the Nepal education sector in general, and in literacy and NFE in particular, have been highlighted in recent studies, discussions, consultations, workshops and reports on education in Nepal. There is general consensus that the capacity of the Ministry of education in general and NFEC in particular is very weak to plan, develop, implement and manage programs aimed at increasing literacy and lifelong education. There is lack of capacity for evidence-based planning and lack of adequate capacity for managing the NFE sub-sector. Nepal is one of the 20 CapEFA countries in the biennium 2009 - 2011 and is being engaged in the capacity development of Non-formal Education staff and CLC management committee members mainly focusing Education Sector Analysis for NFE sub-sector, identification of potential target group and beneficiaries, setting benchmark and target indicator values, and action planning for operationalization of reviewed NFE policy for achieving target indicator values. The outcomes of this effort resulted in the enhancement of capacity of leadership, ownership and harmonization; institutional capacity; organizational capacity; quality and equity; and knowledge-generation for capacity development in the NFE sub-sector as envisaged in Cap EFA Strategic Framework. The concrete and tangible outputs that have evolved so far include: (a) National Plan of Action for developing and expanding CLCs, (b) Establishment of NFE-MIS in three pilot districts, (c) Reliable estimates of current literacy skills through literacy survey. In this context, following a request from the Non formal Education Centre for UNESCO's support in the NFE sub-sector, it has been agreed that UNESCO will arrange for the continuation of support for capacity development in the implementation of the NFE Sub-sector Programme. As such identification of what key capacities are already developed/existing and what additional capacities are needed in the NFE sub-sector in order to enable the country to be on track with EFA goals by 2015 is crucial. Hence UNESCO Kathmandu aspires to further play an active role in assisting the MoE in the area of Literacy and non-formal education. In collaboration with MOE, UNESCO Bangkok, UNESCO HQ, UIL and other relevant partners, the Office will provide support to the MOE for the development of capacity development plan for literacy and NFE subsector in Nepal.

en.full: JFIT Lumbini Project - Phase III

en.value: Lumbini, the birthplace of Lord Buddha, a World Heritage Property, located in Western Nepal, and the landscape surrounding are of outstanding universal value. Two other sites included on Nepal's Tentative Lists, closely related to Lord Buddha's life, namely Ramagrama, the relic stupa of the Lord Buddha, and Tilaurakot, the archaeological remains of ancient Shakya Kingdom. Their safeguarding is important not only for Nepal, but for Buddhists worldwide. Therefore, this JFIT Lumbini project is designed to enable the national authorities to competently protect and manage the Lumbini World Heritage Property and to safeguard the cultural assets of Tilaurakot and Ramagrama.

en.full: Digo Samudaya Eastern DRR Phase III

en.value: Tripartite Agreement sign off – Local Governments, Habitat local Partner and Habitat Nepal, will sign an agreement on funding contributions, roles and responsibilities throughout the duration of the project. • Project Kick-Off Meeting - an orientation about the project with the staff of the partner organisations and local governments to share project objectives with local communities. • Selection of communities - 10 different local communities, 5 in Jhapa and 5 in Saptari, will be selected, in consultation with local government and local partners. • LDMC engagement – The Ward-Level LDMC will be a governmental partner in planning and delivering community-based DR3 interventions along with the NGO partner. • Low-cost, disaster-resilient housing designs – A New Zealand university will be a partner to assist in the technical analysis of low-cost disaster-resilient housing designs developed by Habitat and Municipal engineers. The designs will be incorporated into local government building requirements or codes, and Habitat will support the local government system in monitoring and enforcing these minimum requirements by offering training to governmental staff. • PASSA group formation - PASSA groups with a good representation from the communities, including women and PWD,s will be formed within communities. Habitat Nepal with our partners will facilitate the PASSA members through the eight sessions in the program. PASSA groups will also identify the most vulnerable families within their community, to be eligible for top-up grants. • PASSA training sessions - As an outcome of these sessions, PASSA groups identify the disaster risks facing the communities and suggest the course of actions necessary to mitigate those risks. Similarly, they will discuss various issues related to most vulnerable families, issues of women, PWDs, old age people, children and others. • LDMC/PASSA collaboration – Government and Community groups on DRR join in preparing DR3 projects within the community and how this will be resourced and implemented. LDMC will raise funds and provide technical assistance to the community. • Mason Training- Mason’s are vital to delivering safe shelter in communities in terms of awareness and practice. Masons will be trained on the importance of safe shelter techniques and practice. • Lands Title Office engagement - The local office will be key to owning the joint-titling registration process. Training and process development will be provided through a Civil Rights expert or Lawyer. Having the backing and approval from the Major/Deputy Mayor will ensure greater adoption and acceptance of this new practice. • Women’s Savings Groups to build community awareness of Joint-Titles – The DFAT BPP Micro-Finance project in the same communities uses women’s savings groups to offer and disperse loans to low-income families. These groups of women will receive orientation sessions on Women’s Inheritance Rights and information on fee discounts/exemptions for the new registration process. • Youth Groups to promote Safe Housing and Inheritance Rights – Through local Youth groups and the Habitat Young Leaders Build (HYLB) program, youth will be mobilised to organise community awareness raising events to promote Safe Housing standards and Women’s Inheritance Rights issues. Youth groups will raise resources to conduct these events

en.full: NPL Pooled Appeal Earthquake 2015 SoF: 99700163

en.value: NPL Pooled Appeal Earthquake 2015 SoF: 99700163 On Saturday, 25th of April 2015, a powerful earthquake of magnitude 7.8 on the Richter scale hit Nepal. The epicentre of the earthquake was in Gorkha District, about 80 km north-west of the capital, Kathmandu. The quake was felt as far as Dhaka in Bangladesh and Delhi in India, making it the biggest earthquake Nepal has seen in 80 years. Less than 3 weeks later, another earthquake measuring 7.3 in magnitude struck on Tuesday May 12th with an epicentre southeast of Kodari, in Sindhupalchowk District, 76 km northeast of Kathmandu. The heavy destruction and damage resulting from the first earthquake was further exacerbated as some eight million people across 39 of Nepal’s 75 districts were affected, with 14 districts considered to be the ‘worst affected’.A total of 498,852 houses were categorized as fully collapsed or damaged beyond repair and 256,697 houses were partly damaged, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs. In addition, numerous schools were destroyed and damaged and the earthquakes greatly impacted on public health infrastructures.  As of 30th October 2015, UN OCHA reported that 8,891 individuals lost their lives and 22,309 people were injured.  From that figure, 2,737 children lost their lives and 2,107 children were injured.Save the Children adapted and updated its response projects to ensure they are relevant. One of the major initiatives over the last several months was to focus on beneficiary selection (versus blanket coverage), so that the most affected and marginalized people receive benefits

en.full: COVID-19 Emergency Response and Recovery Project (CERRP)

en.value: Based on the value chain assessment, CRS COVID-19 agribusiness impact assessment study recommendations and GoN (including local municipalities) priorities, CRS Nepal will design and implement an inclusive value chain project in Palpa District. The project will not only address the short-term economic recovery needs of vulnerable households but also make their livelihood more profitable and resilient to future shocks through their integration with value chains. Based on inputs from local municipalities and feasibility assessment, the project will provide support to agribusiness SMEs to recover from the impacts of COVID-19. The support will include improved processing equipment and infrastructure (warehouse, crop storage models, drying yards, collection centers etc.) to agri-cooperatives, farmer groups and/or private enterprises with matching grants from local municipalities and/or province and district level agencies like MoLMAC, ADD and AKC. Priority will be given to functional agri-cooperatives and/or agri-business private enterprises led by women, smallholders or those situated in remote locations. In consultation with the local municipalities, a detailed criteria and process for selection of the agri-cooperatives and enterprises will be developed and implemented. Care will be taken to ensure that agri-cooperatives and enterprises, which are badly hit by the pandemic and are likely to support vulnerable households, are selected. Support will also be extended to youth and returnee migrants on income generation opportunities along the various stages of value chain development for the identified commodities. Key activities will include technical training on select income generation activities such as small enterprises activities, mobile repair, plumbing, grocery start-up etc and provision of a start-up grant to encourage the trained participants to start their businesses. Those trainings will be provided to migrant returnees and vulnerable HHs by keeping 20 to 25 participants in each group based on their choice of training and these trainings will be conducted by technical staffs/consultants hired by partners and contents of those trainings will be based on the need and pre-test result of participants. Convergence with local municipalities will be explored to align with existing youth entrepreneurship development programs like the one being implemented by Tansen municipality. The trained project staff will provide necessary mentoring and troubleshooting support to the entrepreneurs in the beginning phase of their businesses. Markets play a strong role directly and indirectly in the livelihoods of smallholder farmers. The project will identify agribusinesses and SMEs which are critical to the livelihoods of the targeted communities and support them with cash grants and other technical support to help them recover from the impacts of COVID-19 and facilitate market recovery in the process. Other technical support could also include linking businesses with financial institutions for larger credit support, or with suppliers for favorable transaction terms. Where needed, the project will facilitate inclusion of women and other excluded groups into existing agriculture cooperatives and farmer groups to engage in commercial farming activities and increase their income to mitigate recent losses. Inclusion in these groups will also increase their access to various livelihood related government programs and subsidies. The project will provide trainings to targeted households on production and productivity enhancement for the crops/commodities identified through short-duration trainings and on-farm demonstrations where possible. Special attention will be paid to tailor the trainings (timing, duration, location, content, language, etc.) to facilitate meaningful participation from women. Following the trainings, the farmers will be provided with improved production inputs (seeds, planting material, seed treatment material, processing inputs, etc.) to encourage in adoption. These inputs will also help farmers restart their agricultural activities which might have been affected due to a shortage in availability of quality seeds and other inputs due to COVID-19 impact. The project will procure these inputs from local markets and vendors, providing support for the local economy and contributing to market recovery.

en.full: RESILIENT COMMUNITIES THROUGH VULNERABLE EARTHQUAKE RECOVERY (ReCoVER)

en.value: Improving income-generation practices and livelihood skills. Considering the profile of households—  landless, elderly, women-headed households, etc.—and likely wide geographic spread of the targeted  households, ReCoVER will focus on organizing small group trainings, field demonstrations, on-field  mentoring support and digital mediums like radio, which can address barriers like low mobility to build  the skills of target households on improved livelihood production and marketing practices.  To ensure trainings are targeted to the most common needs, and the most likely opportunities for  generating income, CRS will use the early start-up phase of the program to understand specific barriers  that selected vulnerable households face to increasing their income. Considering the COVID-19 context,  and in order to be efficient and safe, area assessments to decide the specific types of livelihood  interventions can mostly be completed remotely, in collaboration with implementing partners and key  local stakeholders like municipalities, agriculture knowledge centers, and private sector actors like local  chambers of commerce, financial service providers, cooperative groups and other value chain actors.  These stakeholders will help ReCoVER leadership tailor production and marketing interventions for the  most practical and applicable production improvements to generate income for households. CRS  technical staff will use the simple guidelines or standard operating procedures that worked in Gorkha  and Okhaldunga, and adjust them to the new working areas using the information gained in the process,  with focus on inclusion of women and vulnerable households. The customized guidance will be rolled out  across staff, partners and local agricultural extension workers to ensure uniform understanding across  program areas. CRS and partner staff will lead trainings on these guidelines through a mix of adultlearning  methodologies like classroom trainings, field visits, farmer exchange visits and practical handson  accompaniment sessions.  Due to the recent decentralization of governance in Nepal, the local municipalities are now responsible  for providing agriculture extension services to communities. The newly recruited and young extension  staff at municipalities will benefit from trainings organized by the program. ReCoVER will work with  municipality extension workers, private sector agricultural vendors and local cooperatives to ensure they  have the skills needed to support ReCoVER livelihood activities. The residual benefit of training these  local stakeholders is that the improved practices remain in the community after the program has ended.  • After building skills of targeted households on improved livelihood practices, ReCoVER will provide  improved inputs to nudge and motivate households in adopting the improved practices to increase  production. Based on experience from Gorkha and Okhaldunga, CRS anticipates that the key livelihood  sub-sectors will be market-oriented vegetable production, backyard poultry, goat rearing and postharvest  management in high value crops like large cardamom and coffee which will contribute to increase  15  in income. ReCoVER will focus on ensuring participants incorporate a few key improved marketing  practices with the aim of bringing their goods to market.

Capacity building initiatives in this project are focused at DDC level and the main areas of capacity building may include but not be limited to: a) Strengthening financial management of DDCs b) Strengthening planning and monitoring capacity of DDC c) Strengthening capacities of DDCs on Information, reporting and documentations. This component is based on the demand of the DDCs and will be implemented in close collaboration with LGCDP.  3.3.2 Component 2: Social Mobilization and EmpowermentSocial mobilization process aims to enable communities to engage in the local level bottom up planning process in order to ensure that they access public resources. This is also a process by which the state can proactively reach to the people. This project will support the districts to institutionalize the social mobilization process in the planning and to enhance the capacity of the social mobilisers.  3.3.3 Component 3: Financial Grant to DDCs  The financial grant from SDC to DDCs will help to deliver services to the citizens, which have generally been too small to bring the long awaited peace dividend to the people. Revenue at the district level (taxes, fee and other service charges) is very little and hence the major source of revenue for more than 80% of the DDCs has been the grants from the central government. The proposed financial support is expected to help DDCs to ease this situation. Any support however, will be linked to improved performance and capacity building of the DDC. The increase in the district budget due to the financial grant is expected to be sustained on the long run because: i) the project will help to double their internal resource (taxes) within five years; ii) the project will help improve their performance and get a better ranking thereby qualify for extra budget from the centre; and iii) the natural increment of the grants allocated by the central government is expected to continue in the near future. These increased resources coupled with the capacity building will ensure the sustainability of the project undertakings once SDC’s support withdraws.

en.full: Strengthening of the Quality Infrastructure for Sustainable Economic Development

en.value: The project is pursuing a multi-level approach to develop relevant quality infrastructure services for businesses. It provides training to the partners’ specialist and management staff in order to strengthen the capacities of organizations as a whole and enable them to be more easily integrated into international networks. The main partner is the Nepal Bureau of Standards and Metrology (NBSM). Further public partners are the Department of Food Technology and Quality Control (DFTQC) and the Department of Plant Resources (DPR). Additionally, the project cooperates with business associations from the pharmaceutical and dairy sectors. A total of three interrelated outputs are targeted: (1) Strengthening the national metrology and QI systems;  (2) Improving the analytical capabilities of the Nepali food authority; (3) Quality assurance in the pharmaceutical sector and in the dairy industry. The project’s objectives are achieved through metrological and analytical lab training, qualifying auditors for specific certifications and accreditations, providing close consultation, and conducting mock audits. Furthermore, the partners are supported through the procurement of selected instruments.

en.value: The intent of our preparedness and response work is to provide immediate life-saving assistance to disaster affected populations with a special focus on children. Save the Children provides support to affected communities ensure effective preparedness systems are in place to minimize the negative effects of disasters on children and their families. It advocates to influence and support key humanitarian actors (donors, government, I/NGOs, Nepal Red Cross Society) to prioritize children's well-being in an emergency.The project will enhance the emergency preparedness and response capacities of Nepal country office, partners and key local authorities in an event of a mega disaster. en.full: Community based Micro Health Project in Nepal

en.value: Input (Project themes and subthemes):                                           Strengthening Health Security Scheme in Nepal (Earlier called as Community-based Micro-health Insurance project in Nepal) has been implemented to strengthen the National Health Insurance Program of Nepal. The interventions are being implemented to support Health Insurance Board (HIB), basically in the areas of policy formulation as well as implementation support in selected districts.  Health insurance program was launched in Nepal in the year 2016 and the program has been expanded up to 58 out of 77 districts of the country by the end of Fiscal year 2019/2020.  This shows the program has covered two-third of the total districts. However, only 8% of the population (18% of the population in program implemented districts) has been enrolled. The program aims to enroll 40% of the population by the next year. The major challenge associated with national health insurance program is the disinterest of people towards health insurance program.  The recent report suggests that almost 2.2 million population were enrolled in health insurance program of which 0.5 million (almost 24% of total enrolled) did not renew their policy. With this trend, it is quiet challenging to achieve the targets of enrolling two-third of the population by 2025 and 100% enrollment by 2030. MISEREOR has been funding the implementation social health security in Nepal since 2010. During the first phase (October 2010- December 2013), pilot project of CBMHI was implemented in two districts (Banke and Dhading) together with a team of Save the Children (SC), Micro Security Academy (MIA), NIRDHAN and DEPROSC Nepal. The project was conceptually new in Nepal and envisioned that the health security schemes helped reduce unforeseeable or unaffordable health care costs through calculable and regularly paid premiums among 45,000 marginal populations in two districts. The second phase (January 2014 to March 2017) of the project was the continuation of the first phase.          Based on the learning of the first and second phase of community based micro health insurance program in Nepal, some issues have been identified, which were proposed for third phase (April 2017 to September 2020) of the program, the issues were:1.          Community scheme should have government registration to get legal standing2.          Provide complete handover of the scheme to the community and local government bodies3.          Continue working together with government on national health security scheme and extend the coverage.

en.full: Post Earthquake Reconstruction Programme in Nepal - Building Back Better

en.value: The 6 year post-earthquake reconstruction programme started in May 2016 at the completion of DFID's humanitarian operations in country.The project in its initial year has provided an array of support to meet immediate priorities of both the GoN's National Reconstruction Authority and vulnerable populations residing in some of the most affected earthquake areas. For example DFID is supporting the Housing Recovery and Reconstruction Platform (HRRP) for coordination and information management of the housing reconstruction sector; activated water and trail related programming in Gorkha, Rasuwa, Dhading and Nuwakot (DFID's focal districts); providing technical assistance to the NRA; supporting a programme on durable solutions for those displaced by the earthquake; contributed resources to the GoN's housing reconstruction cash grant programme for families whose houses have been completely or majorly damaged; enrolling of individuals to the GoN's housing grant programme in 11 most affected districts; geo-hazard assessments of over 500 vulnerable sites; housing damage survey in additional 17 moderately affected districts amongst others.DFID Reconstruction Prgramme team is based in Kathmandu (headead by the Reconstruction Team Leader, Senior Reconstruction Advisor, Programme Manager and a Programme Officer); DFID also has Field Officers based in Gorkha,Dhading, Rasuwa and Nuwakot who are the main district focal points and lead on monitoring activities of DFID's work in the districts

en.full: Sustainable Tourism for Livelihood Recovery Project (STLRP)

en.value: The Sustainable Tourism for Livelihood Recovery Project (STLRP) – a joint project of the Nepal Tourism Board (NTB) and UNDP aims to contribute to the revival of the tourism sector by supporting livelihoods recovery of the most affected workers by providing short-term employment as well as enhancing the capacity of the NTB and other relevant stakeholders to accelerate recovery efforts including supporting the formulation of the National Tourism Recovery Strategy after COVID-19. The project will also initiate activities to support the long-term revival of the tourism sector by creating sustainable jobs and livelihood opportunities in partnership with the private sector; developing human resource capacity; supporting the creation of tourism-based enterprises; strengthening sector-related data and information management and digitalization, and articulating a comprehensive tourism recovery strategy. Aligned with sustainable tourism concepts, project activities will be oriented towards promoting a green economy.

en.full: Strengthening Urban Preparedness, Earthquake Preparedness and Response in Western Region of Nepal (SUPER)
LEAVING NO ONE BEHIND IN NEPAL’S GREEN, RESILIENT, AND INCLUSIVE RECOVERY

en.value: UNDP rolled out a socioeconomic recovery initiative after the COVID pandemic in 2020 in partnership with over dozen local governments. By 2022, the initiative was extended to over twenty-nine local governments. UNDP supported livelihood projects have been implemented in fifteen districts and twenty-nine local government. Over 150,000 people, out of which 51% are women, have directly benefited from these projects. These projects have been instrumental in increasing agricultural production by providing farmers with seeds, tools, equipment, technologies, and skills.

en.full: Prayash: Temporary Basic Income for Marginalized and Excluded Women in Nepal

en.value: The purpose of the Initiation Plan Document is for the UNDP efforts in response to the COVID-19 and to  quickly get off the ground an urgent intervention to provide a temporary basic income for marginalized  and excluded women in Nepal in collaboration with the local government and conduct the feasibility  study on basic income for women in Nepal. The project contributes to the UN Nepal Framework for  Responding to the Socio-Economic Impacts of COVID. The initiatives undertaken under this project are  expected to inform and support the design of a full-fledged dedicated project reflecting the priorities  determined by the Feasibility Analysis, the priorities of the Government of Nepal, and the lesson learned  from the pilot initiative conducted in selected municipalities. The initiative is expected to provide  support to marginalized and excluded women in Nepal to cope with immediate survival needs and  support to become more economically empowered, informed and resilient to face the evolving COVID  context. The plan will be implemented by UNDP for 18 months.  Agreed

en.full: Promoting Green Recovery Project

en.value: The Promoting Green Recovery Project (PGRP) is geared toward supporting COVID-19 recovery in Nepal. It works with various development partners to provide effective management of health care waste from hospitals to reduce the risk of COVID-19 transmission; support governments at the local level in effective management of municipal waste; and promote sustainable urban mobility through cycling campaign.The project through UNDP’s Rapid Financing  facility in response to catalyze solutions to the pandemic through UNDP's "COVID 2.0" offer - Beyond Recovery: Towards 2030, prioritizes creating employment opportunities and fostering business recovery and green growth in the post-COVID context in line with UN Nepal Framework for Responding to the Socio-Economic Impacts of COVID-19. PGRP contributes to Sustainable Development Goals 1 (No Poverty), 3 (Good health and Well-being), 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), 12 (Responsible consumption and production), and 17 (Partnerships for The Goal).

en.full: Building Hope Along the Karnali River Basin (BHAKARI)

en.value: Bhakari seeks to reach 22,350 households (117,750  people) in the six districts of Karnlai and Sudurpaschim province directly. This will be accomplished through three purposes: increase household level food  access and availability.                     Key activities include; Forging partnerships with government and private actors to  improve access to input and output markets including linkages to agrovets, collection centers,  traders and information exchange platforms,Vouchers for agricultural inputs and/ or small  livestock, andTraining and support for climate-smart perma-gardens.2. improve access to sustainable water sources for productive purposes. Key activities inlcude;Sustainable water infrastructure interventions focusing on  installation, management and maintenance of productive water projects, including multiple use water  systems, rainwater harvesting, irrigation storage and delivery systems,Strengthening capacity for  functional, equitable and sustainable water management practices, and220+ Hardware Water  Projects. Productive Use Water Projects are a complementary activity designed to improve the food  security of communities.3. reduce the impacts of natural disasters, with a cross-cutting purpose on increasing inclusion and  empowerment for marginalized groups. Key interventions will include Formation and mobilization of community first responder/  task force membersRisk assessment and planning, watershed level assessment and planning,  etc.,Disaster risk mitigating structure, bio-engineering and fodder plantation, and (4)  Partnership with the Department of Hydrology and Meteorology (DHM) to strengthen early  warning and weather information systems.Other activities include;Value-based food assistance, meeting 100% of macronutrient  requirements for one month plus other basic needsCash for workValue-based  vouchers (for labor-poor households only), and Government Capacity Building in order to  better manage local emergency response and disaster funds.Program activities will adhere to a Gender and Social  Inclusion (GESI) First approach.

en.full: Promoting Economic Resilience of COVID-19 Affected Vulnerable People  (PERCAV)

en.value: Activity 1.1 Understanding the enterprise need of project participants for self-employment.The project will conduct intersectional study which will provide the information on the most vulnerable groups present in the local government. Identification of project participants who will be engaged in self-employment (100% women and PWD) will be done as per the criteria specified in below section of beneficiary details. The assessment of areas of interest and knowhow of project participants towards self-employment will facilitate in designing the customized capacity building interventions for the participants. The process will ensure that the women and other marginalized groups are selected for economic empowerment. Activity 1.2 Capacity building of project participants in entrepreneurship skill, enterprise development and marketingThe project will develop a short-term practical based Business Induction Package including customized MEDEP’s Start and Improve Your Business Modules, skills for business start-up, women in business, investment analysis, market analysis, access to finance and risks and its mitigation measures. A ToT will be given to staffs on the effective delivery of the Package. The trained project staffs will then conduct session with the project participants in the Package thereby capacitating them in entrepreneurship, enterprise development, and marketing. Activity 1. 3 Conduction of training on technical skill-based training and providing necessary start-up support to project participants to operate the enterprise of their choice and knowhow.The project participants will be provided with technical skill-based training to in the enterprise of their choice and knowhow and can include both on-farm and off-far enterprises such as poultry, tailoring, retail shops, restaurants, honey, non-timber products, pig farm, spice cultivation, goat rearing, vegetable farming, shoe making, handicraft etc. The training will be provided through relevant service providers. These trainees will later be supported with required materials and input support to start/strengthen their enterprises. Regular coaching and mentorship to the entrepreneurs will be done by project staffs for smooth start-up and guidance and motivation for successful operation which will provide them with income generation. Activity 1.4 Facilitation in formalization of enterprises for greater access to investmentFacilitation will be provided for registration of the enterprise in relevant agencies. Further, linkages of entrepreneurs with financial institution, local government and Cottage and Small Industries Development Board will be done for resource leveraging. Similarly, the entrepreneurs will be supported in business plan development for obtaining financial loans. These will support entrepreneurs to greater access of resources, services, and finance. Activity 1.5 Facilitation in integration of the enterprise’s product in the value chainThe entrepreneurs will be facilitated to get linked to their respective value chain actors for sourcing of input materials and market of their product. This will include linkages events with market actors, market visits by entrepreneurs, collective marketing, and market sensitization. Activity 2.1 Strengthening leadership and decision-making skills of women entrepreneurs.Development of a concise short-term (1 day) Agency-based Women Empowerment (AWE) package with be done with expert’s inputs. The AWE package will have content on self-realization, leadership, and decision-making skills. ToT on AWE will be provided to project staffs who will then conduct the AWE package session among the women entrepreneurs. This package will motivate the entrepreneurs on taking entrepreneurship roles and empower them in leadership and decision-making skills. Activity 2.2 Sensitization of COVID preventive measures and gender equality among HHs of project participants by mobilization of women volunteersWomen volunteers such as Female Community Health Workers, Human Right Defenders will be engaged in sensitization of project participants household members in gender equality. ToT to women volunteers on gender sensitization and counselling sessions as well as COVID preventive measures to be delivered to participants household members will be done. After training, these trained women volunteers will go door to door of participants house and do the counselling to the family members on gender equality as well as COVID preventive measures. This intervention will support in greater realization on gaps in gender roles and motivate them to support each other. Activity 2.3 Conduction of community gender awareness and GBV sensitization campaignMass campaigning can be an effective means to sensitize communities in gender equality and GBV issues. IEC materials including print materials, public service announcements, video messaging/digital stories will be developed and rights for broadcasting will be obtained. Disseminated will be through appropriate media including social media posts and radio stations. Similarly, Day Celebrations will be conducted in specific days. These events will support in sensitizing communities on gender equality and gender-based violence. Activity 2.4 Advocate and facilitate LGs to have gender equality and social inclusion policies and programsPolicy mapping will be done that will allow to know the gap in gender equality and social inclusion related policies of LGs. Policy dialogue will be conducted with mobilization of women activists and DPOs for obtaining commitment in gender equality and inclusiveness by LGs. These LGs will be facilitated in development of gender and social inclusion policy (where not present) in consultation and inputs from women activists and DPOs. The endorsement and implementation of the policy by LGs will be a milestone in the area of GESI. Further, the facilitation in conduction of gender sensitive and inclusive budgeting workshop will be done. These events will support development and implementation of more inclusive programs that will have a long-term effect on GESI issues.   Activity 2.5 Strengthen the GBV control networks of LGsThe project will collaborate with local government to strengthen its GBV control networks. The local governments have provision of formation of GBV control networks at municipal and ward level, however, the formed networks needs more capacity building for active functioning. The project will held dialogue with district agencies for initiation in mobilization of these networks and support to provide the network members with trainings and necessary skills wherever needed to make the network functional so that it can serve the community effectively. The project will also work jointly with Judicial Committee of the LGs in capacity building of the committee members and strengthen the GBV fund wherever required. The women cell in respective LGs will also be supported to strengthen its functionality. Activity 2.6 Provide targeted support including assistive devices to PWDDisabled Peoples Organizations (DPOs) will be engaged to make assessment of PWD status in project areas. The assessment will provide the categorization of need-based support required for identified PWDs in working area. The project will provide targeted support to some of the most vulnerable PWDs. Activity 3.1 Facilitate to develop economic recovery plan to address the impact of COVID-19 pandemicLGs are provided with responsibility and authority to manage the COVID-19 pandemic. The project with inputs from experts, will facilitate LGs to come up with economic recovery plan to address the impact of the pandemic.  This plan will consist of various strategies including provision of stimulus package and food security through the dissemination of climate change adaptation technologies. Activity 3.2 Collaborate with LGs to initiate establishment of community infrastructureThe project will collaborate with LGs to identify the need for community assets especially agriculture related infrastructure focusing on access to irrigation facilities and an agriculture resource centre. A joint fund with LGs will be created to invest in some of these collaborative initiatives on the establishment of identified community assets. These will provide necessary facilities to increase agricultural productivity that will support in  economic recovery. Activity 3.3 Collaborate with LGs in emergency preparedness and response to stop the spread of COVID-19 infectionThe project will collaborate with LGs and provide necessary PPEs and medical supplies to manage local isolation and health centres. This will support the LGs in better management of spread of COVID-19 infection.

en.full: SASEC Highway Enhancement Project

en.value: The project road is a two-lane carriageway and carries about 14,000 vehicles per day. Traffic is forecast to reach 48,800 vehicles per day by 2041. The road will be median-divided and provides service lanes, footpath, and cycle lane in urban areas. Through the project, the road will be upgraded to a two-lane dual carriageway to accommodate the increasing traffic demand, with improved geometry, pavement, drainage, road safety, and climate- and disaster-resilient features. Grade separation or traffic signal will be adopted at junctions to improve safety for vulnerable road users including women and children who are more likely to walk, cycle or use public transport. River training and bank protection works will minimize the risk of erosion. The project design incorporates lessons from previous projects, including readiness, procurement, asset management and sustainability.

en.full: Implementation of Codex standards to support containment and reduction of foodborne AMR

en.value: Activity 1.1 (G): Communication packages, case studies and outreach activities are developed to raise awareness of Codex standards, food safety and one health, and engage policy makers to support application of Codex standards, with a particular focus on the revised Code of Practice to minimize and contain foodborne AMR and the new Codex Guidelines on Integrated monitoring and Surveillance of Foodborne AMR, as examples of a One health approach.Activity 1.2 (G) A series sustainable training programme, through the holding of several events and tutored courses, is developed to increase capacities at country level to understand and use Codex standards and collect and analyse data on the use and impact of Codex standards, with a particular focus on AMR.Activity 1.3 (G): A mechanism to systematically collect and analyse data on the use of specified Codex standards and assess their impact is established, feeding into the M&E framework of the Global Action Plan on AMR.Activity 1.4(G/R/C): A Global Tool to monitor implementation of AMR-relevant Codex standards into regional and national legislation is developed and piloted at the regional and national levels.Activity 2.1 (G): A set of practical tools are developed to support Member countries in their efforts to apply the Codex Guidelines for integrated monitoring and surveillance of foodborne AMR and related standards.   Activity 2.2 (R/C): A situation analysis and assessment of targeted countries’ surveillance capacities related to AMR is carried-out, using existing assessment tools (e.g.,FAO-ATLASS, etc.) and a plan for costed adjustments to the targeted countries' current surveillance system is provided, based on a collaborative, risk-based approach and in line with country needs.  Activity 2.3 (R/C): Capacities for monitoring and surveillance systems of foodborne AMR in targeted countries, together with tools and guidance on establishment of such systems are strengthened (including reagents to perform AST/bacteriology). Activity 2.4 (R/C): Residue monitoring laboratory network is established to strengthen capacity for monitoring and surveillance systems of foodborne AMR in targeted countries.Activity 2.5 (G): The operationalization of national surveillance networks is supported, including the capacity development and support to Members to collect submit data to InFARM.Activity 3.1 (G): A set of practical tools are developed (including through the revision of practical guidelines and protocols being applied in countries), taking into account the most recent scientific developments, to provide Member countries with comprehensive resources to support their efforts to apply the relevant Codex standards such as the Code of Practice to minimize and contain foodborne AMR and related standards.  Activity 3.2 (R/C): Targeted countries’ capacities are assessed using available tools (i.e., situation analysis; the progressive management Pathway tool on AMR - PMP) to identify their specific needs in relation to managing the risks posed by foodborne AMR, including through the review of policy and legal frameworks, the control functions, the interactions with stakeholders and the science and knowledge base. Activity 3.3 (R/C) Targeted countries are supported to adopt best practice in key areas of foodborne AMR based on existing tools and international guidance.Activity 3.4 (R/C) Selected country’s Regulatory frameworks in the food and agriculture sector are assessed and strengthened, in line with the Codex COP to minimize and contain foodborne AMR, and other relevant Codex guidance.

en.full: Peacebuilding and collaborative leadership, phase 1

en.value:
Catalytic funding is sought for two activities related to the transition from the needs assessment to a longer term  programme of activities through the UNDP’s CLD Programme:

	 

	A.      Three consultative workshops in March on collaborative leadership challenges in Nepal, targeting youth, women, and political party actors.   

	B.      The development and early implementation by the CLD Programme staff of a detailed two-year plan of action based on the CLD needs assessment, including a national mapping of all related donor-funded activities, and including the inputs received from the March consultative workshops.

	 

	Timeline

	Three workshops will take place in March 2011.  The CLD Programme will host a meeting in early April 2011 of all actors, national and international, in order to share findings and support sustained coordination on issues regarding collaboration, leadership and dialogue.

	 

	In April 2011, on the basis of programme planning, the CLD Programme will hire a core team of three to six Nepali facilitators and trainers who can initiate activities. This core team will be needed for at least six months as partnerships with national and local actors as well as government, are established.

en.full: Second Fiscal Policy for Growth, Recovery and Resilience DPC

en.value: The development objectives of the Second Fiscal Policy for Growth, Recovery, and Resilience for Nepal are to: (i) strengthen the regulatory and institutional framework to build back better and greener, and (ii) enhance systems and regulations to protect the most vulnerable and support sustainable business growth. This operation supports fiscal and growth focused reforms that underpin the Government of Nepal (GoN’s) transition to green, resilient, and inclusive development (GRID). Green growth is supported through environmental fiscal policy reforms and support to public investment management. Reforms targeted at strengthening fiscal and debt sustainability as well as the climate resilience of public infrastructure and disaster risk management will enhance overall resilience. Reforms to education, health, and social protection spending will support inclusive growth, while actions aimed at attracting foreign direct investment (FDI) will strengthen aggregate growth.

en.value: 1. Introduction 1.1 Background (300 words) Plan International is a global development and humanitarian organization established in 1937 with a presence in over 75 countries. The organization aims to advance children's rights and promote equality for girls by addressing poverty, violence, exclusion, and discrimination. Plan International Nepal has been working in Nepal since 1978 to help marginalized children, families, and communities access their rights to survival, protection, and participation, with a focus on ending Child, Early, and Forced Marriage (CEFM). Through its project intervention, Plan International in Nepal aims to bring lasting impact in the lives of half a million girls by 2023. Plan International Nepal has made strategic choices based on a wide range of data inputs and global trends, including parenting education and early child development, inclusive and quality education, skill and young women empowerment including Sexual and Reproductive Health Rights (SRHR), child protection, and health, hygiene, and Disaster Risk Reduction and Management (DRRM) support in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic. The organization aims to make an impact on the lives of girls and young women in Nepal by ensuring that its works are equitable, gender-transformative, and protective of human rights. Its humanitarian responses prioritize the needs and rights of girls and young women A 6.4 magnitude earthquake hit the western part of Nepal on 3 November 2023 at 11:47 pm; the largest earthquake to strike Nepal since 2015. Just three days later, there was another strong earthquake with 5.6 magnitude struck. The earthquake has impacted the districts of Jajarkot, Rukum West, Salyan, Dailekh and Rolpa in Karnali province. National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) reported that there has been death of 153 people and 364 people were injured in five districts (Jajarkot, Rukum West, Salyan, Rolpa and Dailekh) and 300,000 people have been directly affected and 62,000 houses damaged[1]. Jajarkot and Rukum West, the geographically remote areas, are the most heavily impacted and have the most damaged houses.  In Jajarkot, 6,768 houses are damaged and 14,997 families have been displaced in Bheri municipality, 6,536 houses damaged and 15,341 families have been displaced in Nalgad municipality and in Rukum West 7,184 houses damaged in Aathbiskot municipality.1.2 Project Rationale (500 words) Affected areas are highly vulnerable to water-borne diseases (Jajarkot district is historically prone to this) and WASH facilities are non-functional. Grains and other food items (normally stored for winter months) have been destroyed. Households in the affected municipalities that rely predominantly on subsistence farming and migratory livelihoods have been greatly affected. As in most humanitarian crises, there has been an alarming rise in gender-based violence and this is an area that requires urgent attention. An estimated 250,000 people, including 80,000 children, require WASH support (UNICEF), including menstrual hygiene materials. Grains and other food items have been destroyed and households relying on subsistence farming are badly affected. People are experiencing significant mental distress and fear for their safety and over 25,000 people, including 8,500 children, require psychosocial support (UNICEF). The proposed targeted areas (Bheri and Nalgaad municipalities in Jajarkot district, and Aathbiskot Municipality in Rukum-West), are identified by the District Disaster Management Committees (DDMCs) of both districts and the UN Resident Coordinator's Office as the most-affected areas. Initial needs identified by Nepal Red Cross Society (NRCS) and the government found an urgent need for shelter and NFIs/cash, safe and inclusive temporary shelter for girls and women, psychosocial support for children, emergency toilets, temporary learning center, transitional shelter in areas and provision of safe drinking water, hygiene kits and dignity kits. Shelter and winterization are immediate urgent needs due to the cold weather in the two targeted districts. Also, there is need of WASH facilities, increased needs for dignity kits for women and Multi-Purpose Cash Assistance (MPCA). These needs are aligned with the SITREP # 4 of United Nations Resident Coordinator Office (UNRCO, Nepal).The proposed intervention will overall contribute to SDG and 15th periodic plan of Government of Nepal. This project aims to implement Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) initiatives that align with the government of Nepal's Fifteen Periodic Plan to reduce losses caused by natural and non-natural disasters. Project closely work with NDRRMA and DDMC.The project aims to contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) targets and goals, particularly Goal 6. Also contributes to 10.8 section of 15th periodic plan Disaster Risk Reduction National Strategic Plan of Action, Priority Action. 3 - Section 6.1.SGD 6: Ensure availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for allSDG 11: Make cities and human settlements inclusive, safe, resilient and sustainableContributes to 10.8 section of 15th periodic planDisaster Risk Reduction National Strategic Plan of Action, Priority Action. 3 - Section 6.1[1] https://reliefweb.int/report/nepal/nepal-western-nepal-earthquake-2023-situation-report-no-03-16-november-2023

ne.full: Enhancing socio-economic condition of deprived communities through collective actions

en.value: The project aims to promote women’s rights, quality education, and resilient communities by addressing systemic inequalities and enhancing community capacities. It raises awareness and builds capacity among women’s groups, activists, and government officials on unpaid care work, gender-responsive budgeting, and programming, while fostering dialogue to advance women-friendly policies. Initiatives include advocacy, campaigns, and evidence generation to reduce gender-based violence (GBV), support survivors, and challenge harmful norms. It strengthens women’s and adolescent girls' agency through advocacy, capacity building, and community mobilization, enabling them to claim rights and challenge structural inequalities.The project also focuses on education, supporting inclusive school infrastructure, teacher training, and eco-friendly initiatives, while engaging child and youth clubs in conservation and resilience-building activities. Evidence-based advocacy for gender-responsive public services and equitable education financing is promoted through partnerships with civil society, unions, and local governments.In building resilience, the project empowers farmers with skills for climate-adaptive agroecology, links them to markets, and supports climate change advocacy. It facilitates disaster risk reduction (DRR) efforts, including establishing early warning systems, prepositioning relief materials, and preparing gender-sensitive guidelines for humanitarian response. By fostering partnerships, generating evidence, and mobilizing stakeholders, the project drives systemic change toward gender equality, inclusive education, and community resilience.

en.full: Green, Resilient and Inclusive Development Program
Nepal Impact Investment Community 2 (NIIC2)

en.value: Nepal aims to graduate from a Least Developed Country status to a middle-income country by 2026. However, low productivity and high unemployment rates have led to large labour out migration and subsequent heavy reliance on remittances. Digital transformation represents an opportunity for a structural transformation of the economy. In Nepal, a rising pool of digital skills and tech start-ups, combined with the growth of small and medium enterprises (SME) in the tech sector, presents an avenue for improving overall economic efficiency and broadening Nepal's export-basket. However, SMEs in the tech sector face challenges, i.e., poor access to finance (debt and equity) and business development services. They represent a negligible portion of Nepali bank and financial institution’s loan portfolio as banks have limited knowledge of this client segment.Nepal Impact Investment Community 2 (NIIC2) is a digital economy focused fund which will facilitate debt and equity investment in digital economy catalysts SMEs in Nepal by attracting investors, i.e. development finance institutions, assisting banks to adapt their loan products to the needs of SMEs in the tech sector, and providing pre- and post-loan business development services to these SMEs. However, the capital requirement for high growth DEC SMEs is such that only debt investment does not suffice and needs to be complemented with equity. Therefore, NIIC2 through its equity fund will enable access to long term patient capital, in the form of equity, for high growth potential DEC SMEs.Digital Economy Catalysts (DEC) SMEs, led by increased private investment, expand market and create jobs and income opportunities for women and men in Nepal, including from discriminated groups.

en.value: The project aims to build target community households’ resilience by mitigating water insecurity and diversifying livelihoods to cope with the impacts of climate change. It will improve watershed management across approximately 200,000 hectares (ha) to mitigate water insecurity and benefit about 50,000 rural households across 24 municipalities and five districts in Karnali and Sudurpashchim provinces. It will invest in (i) 200 small community drinking water supply schemes; (ii) 160 small irrigation schemes; (iii) catchment treatment, including small infrastructure such as filtering dams and bioengineering measures for slope stabilization and stream bank protection; and (iv) the establishment of 60 community-run nurseries, and adopting silviculture principles for barren land plantation and agroforestry. It will support livelihood diversification, with a focus on women, by providing matching grants to promote investments in non-timber forest products (NTFPs), medicinal and aromatic plants (MAPs), and indigenous crops-based enterprises.1 Additionally, it will promote ecotourism by upgrading 57 kilometers (km) of hiking trails and associated infrastructure and support 850 community forest user groups to strengthen climate resilient forest planning through integrated watershed management.

en.value: The Renewable Energy for Resilient Agri-Food Systems (RERAS) project is a joint initiative of UNDP and the Government of Nepal, with funding from Norway, to increase food and nutrition security in western Nepal. RERAS is contributing to SDG 2: Zero Hunger and SDG 7: Affordable and Clean Energy, in Nepal’s most vulnerable regions.   By harnessing the transformative power of renewable energy, RERAS boosts agricultural production and dietary diversity to increase food  and nutrition security. The strength of RERAS lies in its diverse partnerships, bringing together expertise in climate resilient agriculture, off-grid renewable energy, home-grown school feeding and community empowerment.

en.full: Road Safety Management in Nepal

en.value: This project, implemented by United Nations Development Programme and the Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific in partnership with the local authorities, focuses on building the capacity of Nepal's lead road safety agency, the National Road Safety Council, to improve road safety.Road crashes have caused huge loss of human lives and hampered economic growth and sustainable development in Nepal. The number of casualties of road crashes rosed from 1131 in 2008 to 2789 in 2018 with an increase of 146.6%. Experts estimate that if the trend continues, it may reach 4,500 by 2030-2031. In 2017, economic loss due to road crashes was estimated to be 122.88 million USD, around 1.5% of Nepal’s GNP.There are many reasons behind the poor situation of road safety in Nepal. Still, the fundamental one is weak capacity of the National Road Safety Council (NRSC) to function as lead agency on road safety, which is critical for the implementation of the National Road Safety Action Plan (NRSAP 2021-2030).

ne.full: विश्व बैंकबाट हरित, उत्थानशील र समावेशी विकास

en.value: The Green, Resilient, and Inclusive Development (GRID) programmatic Development Policy Credit (DPC) series is a catalyst for Nepal’s ongoing transition to a GRID path. The series of three operations is a key instrument for Nepal to operationalize its homegrown GRID Platform across the economy. This ambition is articulated in the 2021 Kathmandu Declaration on GRID, 2023 Joint Communiqué on GRID, Nepal’s 16th Five-Year Development Plan, and Nepal’s GRID Strategic Action Plan 2024-2034 (SAP) which is now being finalized after a series of provincial consultations. The GRID SAP includes over US10 billion dollars of ongoing and pipeline investments for ten key transitions. The World Bank and 15 other Development Partners (DPs) back this effort, including the International Monetary Fund (IMF), International Finance Corporation (IFC), Asian Development Bank (ADB), the United Nations, and other multilateral, bilateral, and nongovernmental organizations that coordinate on policy, knowledge, and investment via Nepal’s GRID Platform. Nepal’s political situation remains fluid, yet commitment to GRID and this DPC series has been maintained by four successive coalition governments that have taken office since the November 2022 federal and provincial elections. The current coalition took over on July 14, 2024, led by the two largest parties in Parliament. This change has impacted the provincial government set up. At the sub-national level, funds, functions, and staff are managed by the seven provinces and 753 local governments for which legislation, institutions, and administrative procedures have been formalized as constitutionally prescribed. The federalization process is supported by this DPC series.

en.full: Finance for Growth Development Policy Credit (DPC) - III

en.value: The objective of the Third Nepal Finance for Growth Development Policy Credit Program is to support the Government of Nepal in its efforts to strengthen financial sector stability, diversify financial solutions, and increase access to financial services. The third Finance for Growth (F4G3) Development Policy Credit (DPC) will support the Government of Nepal (GoN) in its efforts to strengthen financial sector stability, diversify financial solutions, and increase access to financial services. The F4G3 DPC, in the amount of US80 million dollars equivalent, is the third in a programmatic series of three operations designed to support the country’s transition to the Green, Inclusive and Resilient Development (GRID) pathway, as announced in the Kathmandu Declaration of September 2021. The closing date is April 25, 2025. The proposed F4G3 DPC supports the approach taken by the GoN to return the economy on a post-pandemic recovery path in line with the GRID framework adopted in 2021. Pillar I of the proposed operation promotes resilience by supporting the institutional capacity of the Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB) to oversee the banking sector and by increasing public accountability of the banking sector for climate-related risks. Pillar II opens capital, insurance, and disaster risk markets and fosters financial product innovations. Pillar III extends financial inclusion and improves ease of business-to business and household-to-business transactions. The gender gap in access to digital financial services is addressed via a combination of reforms, specifically targeting women and women entrepreneurs. Climate agenda is fostered through enhancement of supervision of climate-related risk by financial sector regulators and by creating enabling environment for issuance of green financial products in line with the recommendations of the Nepal Country Climate and Development Report (CCDR) (2022).

en.full: Fostering COVID-19 Recovery and SDG Implementation Through Local action in Asia-Pacific, Arab and African countries

en.value: Cities have been and still are the epicenter of the COVID-19 pandemic. The UN Secretary General’s policy brief on COVID-19 in an Urban World indicates that 90 percent of COVID cases were reported in urban areas in July 2020. The size of their populations and their high level of global and local interconnectivity have made cities particularly vulnerable to the spread of the virus. Economic losses due to the pandemic have far wider-reaching impacts than on their immediate populations. UN-DESA’s policy brief (Achieving SDGs in the wake of COVID-19: Scenarios for policymakers) notes that due to economic decline, cities and local governments may, according to estimates, lose on average between 15 percent and 25 percent of their revenues, affecting their ability to provide basic services. There are strong links between the COVID-19 crisis and the achievement of the SDGs. UNDESA’s another policy brief (Impact of COVID-19 on SDG progress: a statistical perspective) notes that the “pandemic abruptly disrupted implementation towards many of the SDGs and, in some cases, turned back years of progress.Since COVID-19 affects urban neighborhoods and groups of people in cities differently, addressing it requires a granular, localized understanding of cities and local realities. Meanwhile, according to the OECD, at least 65 percent of SDG targets will not be reached without proper engagement and coordination with local and regional governments. Thus, effective recovery from COVID-19 coupled with the achievement of SDGs requires increased localized action. SDG localization is hence understood as the process of transforming the Global Goals into reality at the local level, for local communities and their environments, in coordination with national frameworks; a two-way process where the local meets the national and the global and vice-versa.Multilevel governance is a key to ensuring recovery and creating resilient cities. Cities do not work in isolation – on one hand, they are locally responsive and well positioned to put communities’ specific needs at the center of the response and development, and on the other, they are channels for the local implementation of national priorities. National governments set national policy agendas, but their effective implementation highly depends on localization mechanisms, by listening to cities, planning along with them and by systematically including communities into decision-making. In practical terms, when it comes to technical support at city level, the projects adopt UN-Habitat’s comprehensive approach to SDG localization, anchored on three key pillars: i) the Global Urban Monitoring Framework; ii) Voluntary Local Reviews; iii) SDG Cities. Through this approach UN-Habitat and the implementing partners will be able to connect all component of the SDG localization chain – from the collection and management of data to the identification of development gaps and the design and implementation of transformative projects. In addition, implementing partners have past and ongoing experiences in promoting SDG localization sustainable development at local level and have developed respective guidelines to support cities in developing their own Voluntary Local Reviews (VLRs). The project builds on the experiences and knowledge of the implementing entities and aims facilitating the convergence of methodologies into a single joint approach, hence ensuring cooperation and coherence of UN support to both UNCTs and local partners. Such an approach will be reflected in the SDG Localization-COVID-19 tool.
